RECOGNIZING NATIONAL BREAD
MONTH
(Mr. JOYCE of Pennsylvania was recognized to address the House for 5 minutes.)
Mr. JOYCE of Pennsylvania. Mr.
Speaker, today, I rise to recognize November as National Bread Month and
to honor the dedicated men and women
of America’s commercial baking industry who work tirelessly every day to
feed our Nation.
As we enter the holiday season, families across Pennsylvania and throughout our country are turning their focus

towards gathering around the table together, and America’s baking industry
helps make these celebrations so memorable.
The baking industry also strengthens
our community, and Martin’s Famous
Potato Rolls is a shining example of
that. Founded in Chambersburg, this
family-owned business has grown its
reach around the world while remaining true to its roots.
Under the leadership of president
Tony Martin, executive vice president
Joe Martin, guided by the legacy of
their parents, Jim and Donna Martin,
the company continues to invest in the
people of central Pennsylvania.
As a doctor, I know that nutrition
must be accessible and affordable.
Bread is a vital, nutrient-dense staple
that delivers nearly 40 percent of the
dietary fiber in the American diet,
along with essential vitamins and nutrients.
As co-chair of the Congressional Baking Caucus, my responsibility is to ensure that the voices of our bakers, our
millers, and our farm families are
heard here in the Halls of Congress.
Join me in recognizing November as
National Bread Month.
RECOGNIZING TOM CAULFIELD

Mr. JOYCE of Pennsylvania. Mr.
Speaker, it is with respect that I stand
to recognize Tom Caulfield for a truly
inspiring personal and professional
commitment to our Nation’s veterans
and to their families.
Tom has dedicated his career to serving veterans, individuals with disabilities, and their families through his
workforce
development
and
his
mentorship.
A United States Army Vietnam-era
veteran, Tom is the founder and CEO of
Johnstown-based Veteran Community
Initiatives, known as VCI. Under Tom’s
leadership, VCI has expanded its facility and its service offerings to create a
centralized hub for veterans’ assistance.

Tom’s dedication and advocacy has
shaped VCI into a leading resource for
veterans and their families throughout
the region, touching the lives of more
than 15,000 veterans and family members since the organization’s founding
in 1993.
As Tom prepares for his retirement
at the end of 2026, I express my personal appreciation for his remarkable
legacy of commitment to strengthening our veteran community.
RECOGNIZING VOLUNTEER FIREFIGHTERS

Mr. JOYCE of Pennsylvania. Mr.
Speaker, during my time in the district
throughout the month of October, I
visited firefighters at multiple stations
that serve the 13th Congressional District of Pennsylvania.
Repeatedly, firefighters at all volunteer stations have told me that their
greatest challenges relate to recruitment and to funding.
According to FEMA, nearly 97 percent of the Commonwealth’s 1,800 registered fire departments are staffed
fully or partly by volunteers. This is
the third highest percentage in the
United States.
Since 2008, the number of volunteers
nationwide has decreased by approximately 25 percent, while call volume at
the same time has risen by 70 percent.
These statistics deepen the appreciation
for
volunteers
like
Brent
Strasbaugh who serves as president and
firefighter with the Cashtown Community Fire Department in Adams County. Over 30 years of volunteer service,
Brent estimates that he has responded
to more than 2,000 calls while serving
in numerous frontline and administrative positions.
To all volunteer firefighters who
dedicate their lives to the protection of
life and the preservation of property
throughout the 13th Congressional District, I express my heartfelt thanks.

RECOGNIZING ALL VETERANS ON
VETERANS DAY
(Mr. COURTNEY of Connecticut was
recognized to address the House for 5
minutes.)
Mr. COURTNEY. Mr. Speaker, in a
couple of days, our country will pause
on one of the 12 national public holidays, Veterans Day, to recognize the
sacrifice and service of veterans, both
living and deceased, which is the mandate of Veterans Day.
Veterans Day first appeared in this
country on November 11, 1919, when
Woodrow Wilson issued an executive
order decreeing that Veterans Day
would be celebrated on that day, and in
1938, Congress moved and actually
made it a national holiday.
Again, there are a lot of ways people
can participate in Veterans Day. They
can attend veterans ceremonies. They
can attend veterans parades. They can
express vocally their support and appreciation for veterans in their communities.
But all of us have a duty to do more,
particularly here in Congress, to provide support for veterans. As Abraham
Lincoln in his second inaugural address
said: We have a duty to care for the
veteran that has borne the battle; in
other words, provide real, tangible support, both in terms of healthcare and
financial services.
In a couple of days, Congress is going
to have an opportunity to follow
through on that mission that Abraham
Lincoln announced so many years ago
when Congress finally takes up the
Richard Star Act for passage here in
the House of Representatives. Again,
this is a bill which will end one of the
gravest injustices in the Veterans Administration’s system of benefits where
veterans, who have earned a pension
and have earned a disability benefit because of a service-connected injury, are
no longer going to be subject to an offset which reduces those benefits which
they earn.
Again, H.R. 2102 will be up for consideration because of a discharge petition
to finally end this injustice, which veteran service organizations of every
stripe have come to Washington year
in and year out to point out the blatant unfairness to people, who have
worn the uniform of our country and
actually suffered combat-related injuries, being denied the full scope of retirement benefits that they have
earned as well as the disability benefits.
Again, this is an issue that should
unite both sides of the aisle when Congress takes it up pursuant to the discharge petition. Over 300 Members have
cosponsored this bill here in the House
of Representatives. There was an attempt to sort of tweak it and mangle
it, which failed earlier in this Congress,
and on Wednesday it will be time to finally pass a clean Richard Star Act,
which veterans all over this country
are going to be watching closely to
make sure that their Members have listened to them and moved forward in

terms of making sure those veterans
get their full support and benefits, as
Abraham Lincoln said, having borne

Again, I implore all of my colleagues
on Wednesday when this measure
comes up to vote ‘‘yes,’’ send it to the
Senate, get it to the White House, and
end again this unjust concurrent benefit offset.

RECOGNIZING THE PUBLIC TIMBER
PROJECT
(Mr. HILL of Arkansas was recognized
to address the House for 5 minutes.)
Mr. HILL of Arkansas. Mr. Speaker, I
rise today to recognize The Public
Timber Project, a stewardship-rooted
nonprofit dedicated to maintaining the
public hunting lands across our Nation.
As an avid hunter and outdoorsman,
I have spent many days enjoying my
home State, The Natural State, and
what it has to offer our hunters.
I have seen our beautiful lands flooded with trash and debris along the
ramps, the lake banks, and more.
The Public Timber Project works
alongside other nonprofits, like Delta
Waterfowl and Ducks Unlimited, and
they have drastically improved our
Federal refuges and State-owned wildlife management areas through their
advocacy campaign: Restoring Our Refuges.
Each year, more than 69 million
Americans visit America’s 573 national
wildlife refuges. These visitors sustain
waterfowl hunts like the White River
National Wildlife Refuge in Arkansas.
The Public Timber Project didn’t
simply notice the deterioration of
these areas. They took action and
made a difference, devoting over 2,000
volunteer hours, completing 28 site
cleanups, and over 100 boat ramp cleanups.
This is the kind of volunteerism that
is recognized in the State of Arkansas.
HONORING LOWELL BAIER

Mr. HILL of Arkansas. Mr. Speaker, I
rise today to honor the life and legacy
of my good friend, Lowell Baier, who
passed away last year at the age of 85.
Lowell lived what Theodore Roosevelt called the strenuous life, a life
measured not by comfort but by effort,
risk, and service.
His accomplishments outside conservation alone would fill most careers.
He was an Eagle Scout at 14 and a page
in the U.S. House at 16.
He became a successful attorney, real
estate developer, an award-winning author of six books, and a great storyteller who loved talking about the
night he slept on Johnny Cash’s couch
or the time he befriended a Texan
named Willie in a bar, long before the
red-headed stranger was a household
name.
But Lowell’s most enduring legacy is
his love of America’s natural heritage
which he championed, the habitats he
preserved, and the wildlife he protected.
Lowell grew up on a northern Indiana
farm and on his grandfather’s Montana

ranch, and those early years in wild
country never left him.
He spent decades active with the
Boone and Crockett Club, eventually
serving as its president.
He advised American Presidents on
wildlife policy and wrote several books
on conservation, including what was
the definitive history of the Endangered Species Act.
He led the fight to save Theodore
Roosevelt’s Elkhorn Ranch, raising $6.5
million to protect the land that Roosevelt once called ‘‘the cradle of conservation.’’
Lowell was the man in the arena,
whose face was marred by dust and
sweat, who lived with enthusiasms and
great devotions. He was a great friend
and a great mentor. He will be missed.

HONORING GUS ‘‘BUDDY’’ BLASS II

Mr. HILL of Arkansas. Mr. Speaker, I
rise today to recognize the late Gus
‘‘Buddy’’ Blass II of Little Rock, a soldier, a Scout, a leader in the community, and an Arkansan through and
through.
On the 50th anniversary of World War
II, he wrote a memoir for his grandchildren to pass on his idealism and his
love of country. It was his reminder to
them to always cherish the freedoms
that we enjoy and to never forget
them.
Today, I have the distinct honor of
entering his wartime memoir in our
U.S. CONGRESSIONAL RECORD.
Gus was a recon trooper in World
War II, a role that required him to slip
behind enemy lines, gather intelligence, and find his way back.
In a daring act of valor, he and one
other soldier took out a German Tiger
tank while the enemy troops dined in a
nearby restaurant, saving the entire
town.
He was at the Battle of the Bulge and
helped take the town and was the first
to enter Cologne. He was awarded the
Purple Heart for his wounds and brave
service to our Nation.
After serving his country on the battlefields of Europe, Gus returned home
and served the people of Arkansas.
He founded the Community Chest in
Little Rock, which grew into the

United Way. He served on the University of Arkansas Board of Trustees.
I include in the RECORD an excerpt of
his memoir.
GI JOE FROM 1941 TO THE END OF WORLD WAR
II
It all started so innocently. I was 18 years
old and a student at the University of Arkansas in the autumn of 1941. My buddies and I
had driven home to Little Rock for the
weekend. I tell the story that we came home
in a third-hand car since no one in our group
could afford a second hand car. This one was
a Terraplane, which soon went the way of
the Hudson, Hupmobile, DeSoto and Nash.
I had traveled home specifically for my
grandmother’s birthday party on December
6. She was Mrs. Gus Blass and I always felt
I was her favorite grandson because I was
named after her husband. Mrs. Gus Blass was
a wonderful person, refined, ever smiling,
gracious, a good cook who always had special
lunches and dinners when someone came
home on certain occasions, like a visit from
college.
On December 7 we were returning to Fayetteville and stopped at Conway to call home
to confirm news that the Japanese had just
bombed Pearl Harbor. All of our big battleships had been repeatedly hit. The Arizona,
Utah and Oklahoma on battleship row were
lost, along with several others. We later
learned that the Pennsylvania and West Virginia were sunk, but in shallow water and
could likely be salvaged later. The Tennessee
and Maryland were damaged. The Nevada was
beached, but later salvaged. My father said
that an announcement about a declaration of
war was imminent.
We students got back in the old car and returned to Fayettevil]e. We were all in Reserve Officers Training Corp, known as
ROTC. Being a land grant college, the University at that time required ROTC of all its
young male students. There was a patriotic
urge in us to rush right out and enlist in one
of the services. But, after discussing it with
my family and faculty advisor, I decided to
remain at the University, finish the semester
and complete the military training that I’d
already started.
Suddenly, our nation was at war. I remember men appearing in uniforms, shipping out,
draft boards being set up and draft numbers
and classifications being assigned. Women
went for the men in uniform. A man of military age and not in uniform was looked on as
a 4F, or slacker. Those categorized 4F
couldn’t pass the physical and a slacker was
regarded as someone pulling strings to stay
out of the service.
The slogan to keep the world safe for democracy quickly caught on and was about
all that was needed to arouse patriotism and
idealism to the point that all Americans
wanted to do something. The old World War
I marching song, ‘‘Over There’’, stirred everyone’s emotion, as did ‘‘God Bless America’’. No one could sing the latter with as
much feeling as could Kate Smith.
Rationing was a big thing. Families got
booklets of stamps, some for sugar, others
for food, shoes, tires and gasoline. The more
important a worker was to the war effort,
the more gasoline ration stamps he received.
That spring people began planting victory
gardens for additional foodstuffs. In what
used to be a flowerbed in the back yard, now
vegetables grew. The office of price controls
(OPA) was on everyone’s lips. Prices were
frozen on about everything. Most boards
were made up of women and older men. My
mother was in charge of the Red Cross here
in Little Rock. One group made and rolled
bandages, another group knitted socks and
scarves.
Everyone was war conscious. I remember
the top radio program was Hit Parade, spon-

VerDate Sep 11 2014

08:32 Nov 10, 2026

H6083

sored by Lucky Strike cigarettes. In those
days the Lucky Strike package was predominately green. The green dye was needed for
the war effort, so Luckies changed its package to red and white and used the motto,
‘‘Lucky Strike Green has gone to war.’’
I remember the number one song was ‘‘I’ll
be home for Christmas’’. Of course, I would
later spend two Christmases in the army in
Europe. For me, home seemed very far away
both those yuletides.
TRAINING FOR WAR

After semester, we all were shipped to
Camp Walters, Texas, about 140 miles from
Dallas for 16 weeks of basic training, The
barracks, hastily thrown up, were two stories with some 60 men to a floor. We had
cots, footlockers and a few hangers each
under a shelf. It didn’t rain the entire 16
weeks that I was there. I remember we were
listed alphabetically in the barracks, and I
bunked next to Ed Bauer, who was later
killed in the South Pacific. The food wasn’t
all that good, so we would volunteer for KP
(kitchen police), because the mess sergeant
fed his help well.
Basic training involved a lot of hard physical work. We drilled every day but Sunday.
There were classes, films, guard duty, and
the firing range. We marched everywhere we
went. Don’t let me forget the hikes with full
field pack, rifle and equipment. The heat was
always present, so we took salt tablets. After
drilling or marching, we would be soaked in
sweat. Our clothing would be streaked in salt
when it dried.
We had to qualify with both rifle and pistol
on the firing range. One group would be
shooting, while another group marked targets in the pit. If your shot went outside the
circle, the scorer would wave a flag, which
we all called ‘‘Maggie’s drawers.’’
Fall out, fall in, forward, about face, and
halt. We marched and marched. Often, we
sang out our cadence:
‘‘I got a gal in San Antone,
She doesn’t like to be alone.
Hippo, hoppo,
Ring out the moppo
Left oh right, or left.’’
We often marched and sang in cadence
about Chicago:
I used to work in Chicago
In a department store
I did, but I don’t anymore.
A lady came in and asked for a cup
I asked her what kind—at the door
‘‘Mug’’, she said. And mugger I did.
I don’t work there any more.
Sound off!
Woe be to the foul-up. Embarrassment,
extra detail, etc. (example):
Platoon halt! Private Jones, front and center!
Following a snappy salute, ‘‘Private Jones
reporting as ordered sir.’’
‘‘Take hold of your ears, Private Jones.’’
(The GI didn’t seem to understand)
‘‘You dummy, get a tight hold. Now pull
your head out of your rear end!’’
No basic training was complete without a
25 miles hike, full packs, a mortar barrel, or
part of a machine gun. The hike had to be
completed in eight hours. We marched 55
minutes with a five minutes break per hour.
‘‘Get it right the first time men,’’ the sergeant would order. ‘‘Else, you will have to do
it all over again.’’
And the pay! We received $21 a month and
didn’t have any time to spend it. When we
did get a couple of hours off, we were too
tired to go anywhere. The nearest town was
Mineral Wells, but we had no transportation.
A run to the Post Exchange (PX) was possible unless we were restricted to the company area. There was a little recreation area

PO 00000

Frm 00003

Fmt 4634

Sfmt 0634

where we could get 3.2 (percentage of alcohol) beer. It took a lot of 3.2 to give one a
buzz. We were called GI because we were
‘‘Government Issue’’.
Maggie’s drawers, GI, PX and KP. The
military has its own lingo. A ‘‘head’’, or latrine, was a toilet. When ‘‘the eagle flies’’
meant payday. The ‘‘old man’’ was your
commanding officer. He might be no more
than 21, but he was still the old man. The
‘‘C.O.’’ also meant the commanding officer.
The ‘‘top kick’’ was your first sergeant. Your
bunk was called the ‘‘sack’’. The OD was the
officer of the day. The term ‘‘gung-ho’’ was
applied to an overly zealous person or outfit.
Rumors, called ‘‘scuttlebutt,’’ seemed to
abound. From the first day in basic training
and thereafter, scuttlebutt had us shipping
to this place or that when the 16 weeks of
training were over.
The phrase ‘‘Kilroy was here’’ had its birth
during the war. Even civilians picked up on
Kilroy. Snafu (situation normal—all fouled
up) meant a mix-up, and was a much-used
phrase. Brass, or wheels, meant officers.
OFFICER TRAINING

At last, basic training ended. We had earlier thought that, since we’d been in ROTC,
we would automatically progress to officer
candidates’ school, known in military jargon
as ‘‘OCS’’. This wasn’t the case. We first
were selected for OCS. We had to be interviewed by a board of regular officers and
there were written tests to be taken and
passed. Most of us did pass. I recall that all
from Arkansas did.
We were sent to OCS school at Fort Knox,
Kentucky near Louisville for a 15 weeks
course in armor. Not only were those of us
from the University there, but I remember a
number from Louisiana State University and
Texas A&M.
Much of the course was math related to artillery. We learned to fire 75-millimeter
guns, which were then on tanks, and we were
taught to fire the 37-millimeter cannon. We
learned the Browning Automatic Rifle
(BAR), the M1 rifle, .30 caliber carbine, the
rifle grenade launcher, the light and heavy
machinegun, the 81 mm mortar and how to
operate the SCR 536 radio.
We learned how to take weapons apart and
put them together in the dark. This really
helped us later on in Europe. Suppose you
are crawling in the mud and suddenly have
to fire your rifle and it jams. You can’t use
a light or you could give away your position.
So you must clean the weapon and put it
back together while lying there in the dark.
We also learned map reading, fire direction
and plotting coordinates for calling in fire.
I was happy to be near Louisville when the
Kentucky Derby was run. Several of us made
plans to attend the great race since we were
scheduled to be off on Saturday and the
Derby was to run the first Saturday in May.
Would you believe that someone in our group
fouled up and, for discipline, we had to drill
that Saturday from about 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. at
night. None of us got to see the Derby.
We graduated, but there were no commissions in armor, only infantry, cavalry, or
field artillery. I was commissioned in the
cavalry. At age 20, I felt a number of emotions that day. I felt proud, tough, confident,
patriotic, carefree, scared, but glad to get
OCS behind me and to pin the gold bar of a
second lieutenant on my shoulder.
STATESIDE DUTY AS A NEW 2ND LIEUTENANT

After graduating from OCS, I was assigned
to a cavalry unit at Fort Riley, Kansas. At
that time, Fort Riley was America’s headquarters for cavalry and was one of the oldest posts in the country. Fort Riley, still active today, dates back to May 17, 1853. It was
here that the storied 7th Cavalry was formed
in 1867. George A. Custer was second in command of the fort.

E:\CR\FM\K09NO7.004

H09NOPT1

H6084

Located near Junction City, the main fort
is up a hill. We new officers were garrisoned
down in a flat region known as Camp
Funston. We were required to pay dues to the
main officers’ club even though we were not
permitted to go there except at certain hours
or for specific occasions.
We had to look like cavalry officers and
were required to buy breeches, boots, hats,
spurs and carry riding crops. I remember one
night that there was a formal dinner at the
main officers’ club. That evening my friend
Zeke had a date with the general’s daughter.
While dancing, Zeke caught his spurs in the
hem of his date’s long dress just as he
twirled her. Off came her skirt, right there
on the dance floor!
Zeke was a fun guy, tall, angular and
witty. We had been at OCS together in Louisville, where a lot of whiskey is made. At
that time, the distilleries were working
around the clock. One afternoon when we
were on leave in town I asked him,
‘‘Zeke, are you are trying to drink up all
the booze in town.’’
‘‘No chance of that here, Blass,’’ he answered, ‘‘because I got them working
nights.’’
At Fort Riley, I was assigned to the firing
line to train young soldiers to use the M1
rifle. One day a colonel drove up in his jeep
to do an inspection. As he climbed from the
jeep, he caught a spur and fell face first on
the ground. I laughed aloud and promptly
found myself assigned officer-of-the-day duties for the next three weekends.
I taught men to fire from various positions, such as prone, standing and kneeling.
We had several trainees from the Appalachian region of Kentucky and Tennessee.
One boy couldn’t say fire, but instead pronounced the word ‘‘farr’’, as in ‘‘farrwood’’.
The instructor would say, ‘‘Ready on the
left! Ready on the right! Ready on the firing
line. Targets. . .Fire! You weren’t permitted
to shoot, until the command ‘‘FIRE’’ was
given. One day this boy fired prematurely
after I’d only said, ‘‘ready on the left!’’ I
called out, ‘‘who fired that shot?’’ Rather
sheepishly, he looked up from his prone position and answered: ‘‘I farred it.’’

HONORING CONSTANCE ‘‘CONNIE’’
YOUNG

Ms. MEJIA. Mr. Speaker, I rise this

‘‘Connie’’ Young of West Caldwell.
A proud World War II Navy veteran,
Connie enlisted as a Woman Accepted
for Volunteer Emergency Service, otherwise known as WAVES, in the United
States Navy. She served our Nation
well as both a captain’s yeoman at
Hunter College and on an antisubmarine missile project with the Navy’s
Bureau of Ordnance.
Following her service, Connie built a
life rooted in family, education, and
community. She earned her degree in
economics from Saint Elizabeth University, raised four children with her
husband, Roger, and devoted decades to

MARINE CORPS RESERVE ASSOCIATION’S CENTENNIAL
(Mr. BERGMAN of Michigan was recognized to address the House for 5 minutes.)
Mr. BERGMAN. Mr. Speaker, yesterday was the National Veterans Parade.
In fact, two of the three Vietnam veterans still remaining in Congress were
there. My colleague sitting right in
front of me, JIM BAIRD from Indiana,
rode in the parade aboard one of his
weapons trucks, if you will, with some
of his colleagues.

HONORING AMERICA’S VETERANS
(Mr. BAIRD of Indiana was recognized
to address the House for 5 minutes.)
Mr. BAIRD. Mr. Speaker, as my colleague General BERGMAN mentioned, it
was a pleasure to be in the parade yesterday and to have a parade marshal
who was a former Vietnam helicopter
pilot, as was General BERGMAN.
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to honor
our veterans, especially those who
served in Vietnam.
Yesterday, I rode down Constitution
Avenue in the National Veterans Parade aboard a replica of the Vietnamera gun truck, Brutus.
Roger Blink, a driver of the original
Brutus, built the replica that participated in yesterday’s parade. This work
preserves the stories of the men who
defended our convoys and honors those
who never returned.
For me, riding in the parade carried
a deep personal meaning. In Vietnam, I
served with the 523rd Transportation
Company. Our convoys carried vital
supplies along roads prone to ambush.
Soldiers transformed ordinary Army
trucks into gun trucks, adding machine guns, scrounged-up armor, and
layers of sandbags, and we made do
with what we had.
The men operating those trucks
saved countless lives, including my
own.
I was aboard the Proud American,
formerly the Ace of Spades, that was
made by Sammy Seay. It was driven by
Robert Thorne when two rockets
struck in the rear of the truck. Robert
steered us into a mountain rather than
over the embankment.
In saving others’ lives, Robert lost
his own. Other gun truck crews who
had already reached safety turned

PO 00000

Frm 00005

Fmt 4634

Sfmt 0634

around, risking their lives to come
back to save us. Those trucks were Satan’s Lil’ Angel, NCOIC Chester Israel,
and King Kong, NCOIC Danny Cochran.
You never forget courage like that.
Mr. Speaker, as we mark Veterans
Day during America’s 250th anniversary, I ask Americans to remember all
of our veterans who have given so
much for this country. Those who I
served alongside and all of the veterans
deserve sincere gratitude when they return home. They deserve it today and
every day.
Mr. Speaker, I thank every veteran
and servicemember for defending our
freedoms. Honoring our service remains one of the greatest privileges of
my life.

The War Powers Resolution further

granting any authority to the President or to introduce United States
Armed Forces into hostilities which

Accordingly, the reporting and termination procedures subsequently established by the resolution do not
themselves constitute affirmative statutory authorization to commence hostilities. Rather, the introduction of
United States Armed Forces into hostilities must rest upon one of the authorities or circumstances identified in
section 2(c) in order for a conflict to be
considered lawful.

Section 5(b) of the War Powers Resolution of 1973 provides that, within 60
calendar days after a report is submitted or required to be submitted to
Congress by the President of the
United States upon the Executive introducing United States Armed Forces
into hostilities or into situations
where imminent involvement in hostilities is clearly indicated by the circumstances, whichever is earlier, the
Executive shall terminate any use of
United States Armed Forces unless
Congress has declared war or has enacted a specific authorization for such
use of the United States Armed Forces,
has extended by law such 60-day period,
or is physically unable to meet as a result of an armed attack upon the
United States.
Section 5(b) further provides that,
absent a formal congressional declaration of war, specific statutory Authorization for the Use of Military Force or
an extension of the 60-day period enacted into law during that period,
‘‘such 60-day period shall be extended
for not more than an additional 30 days
if the President determines and certifies to Congress in writing that unavoidable military necessity respecting
the safety of the United States Armed
Forces requires the continued use of
such Armed Forces in the course of
bringing about a prompt removal of
such forces.’’

The foreseeable consequences of Secretary Hegseth’s scheme manifested in
the United States strike on the
Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School
which killed and injured more than 200
civilians and exposed systemic failures
in the Department of Defense targeting
process. The events of that strike and
the reported events leading to it are as
follows:
On the morning of February 28, 2026,
at approximately 9:45 a.m. local time,
the United States, in partnership with
Israel, launched Operation Epic Fury
commencing the 2026 Iran war. Within
the first hour of the U.S.-Israeli offensive into southern Iran, three BGM–109
Tomahawk cruise missiles fired from
United States Navy warships impacted
the elementary school between 10:23
and 10:45 a.m. local time.
Because the war was commenced
midmorning on a Saturday, the first
day of the Iranian workweek, students
were in attendance at the school. Despite an attempted evacuation of the
school, at the time of the first cruise
missile’s impact, between 170 and 264
students were present in the facility,
most of whom were girls between the
ages of 7 and 12.
Whereas it is unclear how many casualties were inflicted by the first impact, which caused a partial destruction of the structure and the collapse
of its roof, it is reported that students
were then sheltered in a prayer room
deeper in the facility waiting for rescuers, when a second and a third missile in rapid succession, impacted the
building.
Reported death tolls from the strikes
on the elementary school indicate that
at least 156 civilians were killed, with
some reports suggesting the civilian
death toll surpassed 170. Those killed
include at least 120 schoolchildren, 26
teachers, and 7 parents attempting to
evacuate their children, a schoolbus
driver, a pharmacy technician from a
nearby clinic, and the 6-month-old unborn child of one of the teachers also
killed in the attack. An estimated 95
other individuals were wounded.

Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.

This Act may be cited as the ‘‘Nuclear REFUEL (Recycling Efficient Fuels Utilizing Expedited Licensing) Act’’.

Section 11 v. of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954
(42 U.S.C. 2014(v)) is amended—

and inserting ‘‘(A) separating isotopes of uranium or enriching uranium in the isotope 235; or

Mr. LATTA. Mr. Speaker, I yield myself such time as I may consume.
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak in support of H.R. 3978, the Nuclear REFUEL
Act, which I introduced with the gentleman from California’s 50th Congressional District.
A strong, robust, domestic nuclear
fuel cycle is essential for maintaining
growing nuclear capacity in this country. The deployment of advanced reactors and the operation of our existing
fleet cannot be accomplished without
access to an abundant secure fuel supply.
To assist this important goal, H.R.
3978 advances a policy to maximize access to the additional energy available
in spent nuclear fuel, which retains up
to 90 percent of potential energy for future use.
This legislation does this by clarifying that spent fuel reprocessing facilities would be licensed under the
same one-step framework as other fuel
cycle facilities rather than the longer
two-step process more appropriate for
nuclear reactors and facilities that
produce special nuclear material for
national security purposes.
This bill was thoroughly vetted in
the legislative process in the Energy
and Commerce Committee and was reported, as amended, by unanimous bipartisan recorded vote.
Allowing for a more efficient and predictable licensing pathway for reprocessing facilities supports the pursuit of
this promising technology.
H.R. 3978 maintains nonproliferation
protection and all necessary requirements to assure adequate protection of
the public. It also creates a more efficient path for extraction of certain important isotopes from spent fuel, which
are critical to American space exploration and national security missions.
If our Nation is going to maintain its
lead on nuclear technologies, we must
make maximum use of our nuclear fuel
resources and provide an efficient path
to license promising reprocessing technologies.
I urge all my colleagues to support
H.R. 3978, the Nuclear REFUEL Act.
Mr. Speaker, I reserve the balance of
my time.

Mr. LATTA. Mr. Speaker, I yield myself such time as I may consume.
Mr. Speaker, I rise in support of H.R.
5549, the Efficient Nuclear Licensing
Hearings Act, sponsored by the gentleman from Virginia’s Ninth Congressional District, the gentlewoman from
Washington’s Eighth Congressional
District, and the gentleman from
Texas’ 33rd Congressional District.
This bipartisan legislation advanced
out of the Energy and Commerce Committee unanimously. Since Congress
enacted the ADVANCE Act 2 years ago,
the Nuclear Regulatory Commission,
the NRC, has been hard at work to ensure an efficient, timely, and predictable licensing process.
H.R. 5549 builds on this effort by repealing a 70-year-old provision of the
Atomic Energy Act that is no longer
necessary. This provision requires the
NRC to hold a hearing on licensing applications, regardless of whether a person requests a hearing in the first
place. This original requirement forces
NRC and its staff to spend time and resources preparing for and conducting
uncontested hearings on applications,
basically hearings that nobody requests.
The provision made sense when the
nuclear industry was in its infancy and
the licensing processes were not as
transparent as today. Under current
practice, there are numerous opportunities to participate in the licensing
process and to request hearings.
The NRC staff and commissioners
have for over a decade called for elimination of this provision. By removing
this requirement for an uncontested
hearing, this bill significantly reduces
the time and cost to deploy nuclear energy without impacting safety or public engagement.
Importantly, the bill preserves the
right of any person whose interest may
be affected by a license proceeding to a
hearing.
This legislation, in combination with
the suite of nuclear bills being considered today, will help enable the efficient and safe deployment of nuclear
energy to benefit our society.
Mr. Speaker, I urge my colleagues to
join me in supporting H.R. 5549, and I
reserve the balance of my time.
Mr. PALLONE. Mr. Speaker, I yield
myself such time as I may consume.
Mr. Speaker, H.R. 5549, the Efficient
Nuclear Licensing Hearings Act, would
cut down on red tape by eliminating
the need for the Nuclear Regulatory
Commission to hold a hearing on an application for a license when no one
asked for one, and these so-called mandatory hearings often cost applicants
up to $4 million, costs that are often
eventually passed on to American families across the Nation in their electric
bills.

Mandatory hearings, Mr. Speaker,
date back to an era when we had not
separated out the safety regulation responsibilities that now belong to the
NRC from the policy of promoting nuclear energy that now belongs to the
Department of Energy, and the mandatory hearing, was a tool that Congress
thought necessary to maintain public
confidence and trust in nuclear safety
regulations, especially in an era before
the Sunshine Act and environmental
reviews.
Thankfully, we live in a very different and much more transparent
world today, so these mandatory hearings are not hearings in the sense that
you might think, Mr. Speaker. Instead,
they are purely paper proceedings that
take months to complete happening between NRC staff and reactor developers, not the public. No public scrutiny or transparency is lost by getting
rid of them. Instead, the NRC and its
staff can focus on the issues in an application that really matters.
The NRC recognized this and endorsed the idea 18 years ago. Importantly, this bill does not really touch
another type of hearing at the NRC,
contested hearings, where someone demands that the NRC investigate a specific component of a license application, and communities retain their
rights to demand hearings and community meetings as part of the environmental and safety review processes,
and that is completely untouched.

H.R. 5549 would amend the Atomic

Uncontested hearings are rarely necessary these days. Mandatory hearings

November 9, 2026

CONGRESSIONAL RECORD — HOUSE

08:32 Nov 10, 2026

are relics of the 1950s when the nuclear
licensing processes were created and
every reactor design was novel or different. These hearings were intended to
stress test each reactor design and
have technical experts debate the merits of each project.
When the mandatory hearing was
adopted in 1957, there were no civil nuclear energy reactors operating in the
United States. Today there are 94.
The original nuclear regulator, the
Atomic Energy Commission, was abolished in 1974, yet the mandatory hearings remain.
Uncontested mandatory hearings are
an archaic section of the statute that
was put in because of the newness of
nuclear energy and because of the
then-prevalent procedure-based regulatory structure that emphasized contested hearings, such as those used in
electric rate cases.
Today, the need for uncontested
hearings is not evident and the hearings are simply a waste of resources.
We actually heard testimony at Energy
and Commerce that witnesses said that
the nuclear license applicant pays a fee
over $300 an hour for each NRC staff
member to prepare for the hearing. One
witness said that there could be up to
12 NRC staff at each hearing. As you
can see, Mr. Speaker, that could add up
fairly quickly.
According to one NRC study, on average, a mandatory hearing takes up to
1,000 hours, which is charged to the applicant, and, as my colleague said,
could be $4 million pretty easily.
Each perfunctory hearing costs a licensing applicant that money. Numerous current and former NRC commissioners nominated by Presidents of
both political parties have all agreed
that mandatory hearings are not necessary. The staff have also expressed
support for repealing the requirement,
saying it is unnecessary. Eliminating
the uncontested hearing requirement
would in no way affect public scoping
or siting meetings.
Over the years, the NRC statutorily
authorized Advisory Committee on Reactor Safeguards has taken on more reactor safety review responsibilities.
Additionally, NRC staff independently assess technical data and publish
voluminous safety and environment
data on its public database. Repealing
these hearings would not affect the
right of any affected party to request a
hearing on specific matters.
My bill includes language that specifically leaves open the possibility of
the affected party requesting an
uncontested hearing. The bill also codifies current NRC practices that use informal, nonadversarial hearing procedures.
Finally, the bill requires the NRC to
publish a notice of its intent to issue a
construction or operating license in
the Federal Register at least 30 days
before the license takes effect.
Over the past two Congresses, the
Energy and Commerce Committee has
received testimony showing that re-

transparency and public confidence in
the nuclear industry that we separate
the government agency responsible for
regulating the safety of our Nation’s
nuclear fleet, the NRC, from the part of
the government responsible for promoting nuclear energy, and that is the
Department of Energy.
Both of these agencies have a vital
role to play. The Department of Energy
is making investments in the reactor
designs of the future and helping the
fundamental basic research that will be
vital for our Nation to stay competitive in the coming decades. Meanwhile,
the NRC is responsible for ensuring
that our Nation’s operating reactors
are safe and secure.
As a part of DOE’s mission to promote nuclear energy, Congress granted
it a very limited authority to permit
its own nuclear reactors. These reactors cannot be commercial reactors
that sell electricity. They are typically
novel reactor designs that are thousands of times smaller than the NRC’s
regulated reactors that power our communities and our homes.
Unfortunately, while NRC has taken
a very robust stance toward transparency around the licenses it issues
and its rules, DOE has doubled down on
secrecy. It changed its nuclear safety
rules without alerting Congress, and it
took far too long to be transparent
about the reactor pilot program, which
kicked off last year.
The only way to build public confidence and trust that these DOE-authorized reactors are safe is through
transparency, making authorizations,
safety documents, and alterations to
safety rules public.
This bill, H.R. 9084, the Department
of Energy Nuclear Transparency Act,
brings a reasonable solution to the
table. It would require DOE to make
public announcements every time it
changes its nuclear safety rules, issues
a safety analysis for a proposed nuclear
facility, or grants a proposed nuclear
facility a formal authorization. It
would also require the DOE to develop
a public report detailing all of its authorization activities each year.
These are vital transparency guardrails that can help ensure the success

its new Launch Pad initiative. However, if the Department and the national laboratories running the program are not fully dedicated to transparency, then their efforts are doomed

FACILITIES.

to affect—
(1) the applicability of the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (42 U.S.C. 4321 et seq.)

The deployment of advanced reactors

abundant, secure fuel supply. Increasing this fuel supply requires expanding
the Nation’s capacity for licensing enrichment of nuclear fuels. Licensing
more enrichment is critical for that expansion, especially as we have banned
access to Russian fuels.
H.R. 9612 amends the Atomic Energy
Act to ensure the licensing for nuclear
fuel enrichment facilities aligns with
the more efficient one-step licensing
process for similar-risk uranium conversion and fuel fabrication facilities.
Testimony from industry experts before the Energy and Commerce Committee indicated these provisions could
reduce over a year from the licensing
process. The bill will eliminate unnecessary licensing steps and allow for licensees to construct facilities prior to
licensing under the same terms and
conditions already applicable to the
other types of fuel cycle facilities.
Under this legislation, there would be
no impact on safety assessments or inspections, no impact on environmental
assessments required under the National Environmental Policy Act,
NEPA, nor on any other of the requirements for safeguards and security to
meet the relevant provisions of the
Atomic Energy Act.
This is just a more efficient process.
If we are going to build out our nuclear
industry, we need nuclear fuel. Further, we need a secure, abundant supply of domestically produced fuel.
The American Enrichment Deployment Act helps make a more efficient

Mr. Speaker, there has been a renewed interest in nuclear power that
could lead to a new generation of clean
American nuclear energy. Unfortunately, there is a large barrier in the
way, and that is we simply do not have
enough fuel for the hypothetical reactors.
Since the 1990s, we have seen a reduction in American enrichment capacity
as we spent decades importing enriched
uranium that had formerly resided in
Soviet nuclear warheads. In the intervening years, Russia expanded its enrichment capabilities far beyond its domestic needs and eventually came to
dominate the global enriched uranium
market, including for American reactors.
After Russia’s invasion of Ukraine,
we realized how vulnerable our supply
chains were. I am proud the Energy
and Commerce Committee led the way
on getting several vital pieces of legislation signed into law.
One law bans the importation of Russian uranium, providing certainty to
the American domestic enrichment industry. Another authorized programs
at the Department of Energy that are
designed to inject funding into this sector and quickly enable expansion of domestic enrichment facilities.
Barriers still remain to a healthy domestic enrichment industry, especially
slowdowns to licensing enrichment facilities.
This bill, H.R. 9612, the American Enrichment Deployment Act, addresses
those licensing barriers in a few ways.
First, it makes the process to license
an enrichment facility identical to the
process to license other fuel cycle facilities, like uranium conversion or
fuel fabrication facilities.
Second, the bill explicitly allows any
developer of an enrichment facility to
start constructing their facility before
receiving an NRC license.
Uranium enrichment facilities are essentially large warehouses for centrifuges, and developers need plenty of
time to construct all the nonnuclear
components of the facility. There is no
reason they shouldn’t be able to start
construction just like any other building or project could.
We amended the bill in the Energy
and Commerce Committee, and I think
it is very important to highlight a few
of the changes that were made that are
included in the version of the bill that
we are going to be voting on today.
The bill is now crystal clear. The National Environmental Policy Act, better known as NEPA, still applies to enrichment facilities; anyone has the
right to request a hearing on a facility;
and the NRC still has all its normal
rights to conduct inspections.
All the safeguards we rely on to keep
our homes and communities safe still

Mr. LATTA. Mr. Speaker, I move to
suspend the rules and pass the bill
(H.R. 9613) to update the role of the Advisory Committee on Reactor Safeguards in the licensing and oversight of
nuclear reactor facilities, and for other
purposes, as amended.
The Clerk read the title of the bill.
The text of the bill is as follows:
H.R. 9613
Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in
Congress assembled,
SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.

This Act may be cited as the ‘‘Nuclear Advisory Committee Reform Act’’.
SEC. 2. ADVISORY COMMITTEE ON REACTOR
SAFEGUARDS.
(a) IN GENERAL.—Section 29 of the Atomic En-

ergy Act of 1954 (42 U.S.C. 2039) is amended—
(1) by striking ‘‘There is’’ and inserting the
following:
‘‘(a) ESTABLISHMENT.—There is’’;
(2) by inserting ‘‘(referred to in this section as
the ‘Committee’).’’ after ‘‘Reactor Safeguards’’;
(3) by striking ‘‘consisting of’’ and all that
follows; and
(4) by adding at the end the following:
‘‘(b) MEMBERSHIP.—The Committee shall consist of a maximum of 15 members, to be appointed by the Commission, who shall represent
a diverse background of technical expertise relevant to the mission of the Commission.
‘‘(c) TERMS.—
‘‘(1) IN GENERAL.—Except as provided in paragraph (2), the Commission may appoint a member of the Committee for not more than 2 terms
of 4 years each.
‘‘(2) EXCEPTION.—The Commission may appoint a member of the Committee for more than
2 terms if the Commission determines that there
is a compelling need for the member’s continued
service.
‘‘(3) APPLICABILITY.—This subsection shall
apply with respect to members appointed after
the date of enactment of the Nuclear Advisory
Committee Reform Act.
‘‘(d) COMMITTEE ACTIONS.—The Committee
shall—
‘‘(1) review safety studies and facility license
applications referred to it and make reports
thereon;
‘‘(2) advise the Commission with regard to—
‘‘(A) the hazards of proposed or existing reactor facilities; and
‘‘(B) the adequacy of proposed reactor safety
standards; and
‘‘(3) perform such other duties as the Commission may request.
‘‘(e) FOCUS OF COMMITTEE.—In taking an action pursuant to paragraph (1), (2), or (3) of
subsection (d), the Committee shall, to the extent practicable, focus on issues that—
‘‘(1) directly relate to facility design;
‘‘(2) are safety significant;
‘‘(3) are unique, novel, or noteworthy; and
‘‘(4) have not been previously acted on by the
Committee.
‘‘(f) POLICIES FOR EFFICIENT AND TIMELY ACTION.—The Commission shall maintain and, if
necessary, modify policies to ensure efficient
and timely action by the Committee, including
efficient and timely coordination between the
Committee and staff of the Commission.
‘‘(g) CHAIRPERSON.—The Commission shall
designate 1 member of the Committee as the
Chairperson of the Committee.
‘‘(h) PER DIEM.—The members of the Committee shall receive—
‘‘(1) a per diem compensation for each day
spent in meetings, conferences, or other work of
the Committee; and
‘‘(2) compensation for necessary traveling or
other expenses while engaged in the work of the
Committee.

to deal with licensing issues from
many well-characterized and understood reactors and technologies. However, a new wave of technologies, expected to enter the license process,
would very much benefit from the Advisory Committee’s independent review
and advice.
b 1610
H.R. 9613 serves to update membership requirements in terms of service
and to focus the important work of
ACRS where it will provide greatest
value to the NRC and the public.
The bill directs ACRS to focus on
issues that directly relate to reactor
facility design or safety significant or
noteworthy or novel and have not been
previously acted upon by the committee.
The bill also provides ACRS flexibility to decline and review issues in
applications that do not merit attention, allowing ACRS to follow a more
efficient risk-informed approach to
work.
H.R. 9613 will help ACRS to more efficiently and effectively serve the commission as it reviews nuclear license
applications.
I urge my colleagues to join me in
supporting this bipartisan legislation
to advance our work to ensure the benefits of nuclear energy for our society.

Mr. Speaker, H.R. 9613, the Nuclear
Advisory Committee Reform Act, alters the scope and organization of the
Nuclear Regulatory Commission’s Advisory Committee on Reactor Safeguards, the body that provides independent technical expertise on nuclear
licensing.
Now, 73 years ago, the Atomic Energy Commission created the ACRS, an
expert body meant to enhance the
quality of safety and environmental reviews of applications for nuclear licenses. Soon after its establishment,
Congress passed a law enshrining the
ACRS in statute and requiring that it
review all applications for commercial
nuclear power plants to ensure the
safety of what was at the time a completely new technology.
Seven decades later, the landscape
has significantly changed. Nuclear energy is no longer novel. More importantly, there have been generations of
nuclear experts that now staff the
NRC, in contrast to the small handful
of experts who could inform the work
of the old Atomic Energy Commission
in the aftermath of World War II. But
the requirement that the ACRS review
every single reactor has remained the
same.
But at the same time, getting rid of
the ACRS altogether, as some have
suggested, would be wildly irrespon-

PO 00000

Frm 00023

Fmt 4634

Sfmt 0634

sible. We are seeing a new generation
of nuclear reactors, many with new design elements or aspects that have
never been tested. Independent technical review is vital for public confidence in the safety of these reactors,
and that is increasingly important at a
time when the NRC itself is under attack and becoming more political.
Any alterations to the ACRS must
balance a need for efficiency with a
need not to disrupt an organization
that has helped keep us safe for nearly
75 years. I think this version of H.R.
9613 before us strikes that balance. It
removes the requirement that the
ACRS review each application, while
requiring that the ACRS review the
subset of applications that raise
unique, novel, or noteworthy issues.
Critically, it keeps the ACRS itself in
charge of making the decision about
what is unique, novel, or noteworthy,
not the NRC. The ACRS retains its
ability to investigate issues other than
reactor applications that deserve its
attention as well.
So the idea is to focus the ACRS on
what matters most—issues that have
not come up before that are tricky and
can benefit from a unique technical
viewpoint, and this viewpoint has been
useful in the recent past. The ACRS
has contributed to recent reviews of
the first-ever small modular reactor
and the first-ever restart of a nuclear
power plant.
This bill will help the ACRS continue
its important work into a new generation of reactors, letting its experts
focus on the highest important issues
and ensuring that those experts are
heard in the licensing process.
So I thank Chairman GUTHRIE and
Representative HARSHBARGER for their

path forward for the ACRS that works

The level of expertise demanded by

b 1620
The special workforce and pay authority Congress established for the
NRC in the bipartisan ADVANCE Act
just over 2 years ago sought to help attract and preserve exceptional employees at the NRC.
H.R. 9614 fixes an issue which was inadvertently created with those incentive pay provisions in the ADVANCE
Act. Those provisions left out career
Senior Executive Service, or SES, employees, who typically are managers.
This created potential issues of pay
alignment for exceptional managers
that may undermine effective management and retention.
It is important for quality personnel
at the NRC to ensure efficient licensing
and oversight, especially during this
time of industry growth. This requires
good management.
H.R. 9614 authorizes the Chairman of
the NRC to modestly increase the compensation rate of selected Senior Executive Service employees at the NRC.
This authority to increase the rate of
compensation by not more than 10 percent for certain employees will help
the NRC maintain a strong, specialized
workforce, as well as the quality management necessary to carry out the
NRC’s mission.

good friend, MORGAN MCGARVEY. It has
been a pleasure working with my
friend.
I also thank Senator MORAN for leading the Senate companion to this bill
and the work that he has done to support America’s veterans. Veterans
dealing with service-connected disabilities need this must-pass legislation to
ensure their earned benefits ease their
financial needs.
Many disabled veterans rely on their
benefits to help keep their personal finances in order, such as paying for necessities like mortgages and groceries.
Reducing the financial burden too
many veterans, survivors, and their
families face helps alleviate some of
the stress and anxiety within the veteran community, and passing this costof-living adjustment provides veterans
with the peace of mind they deserve
and access to the benefits they are
owed.
With Veterans Day this Wednesday, I
urge all my colleagues to support this
bill honoring our commitment to serving those who served us.
I thank my colleagues for the compliments and kind words. I have to tell
Mr. MCGARVEY, if nobody was paying
attention, he and I absolutely proved
that if you sit down and take the time
to learn each other, you can absolutely
work hand in hand to get things accomplished in this amazing place that
we sit in today.

CONGRESSIONAL RECORD — HOUSE

Mr. MCGARVEY. Mr. Speaker, I yield
2 minutes to the gentleman from New
Jersey (Mr. CONAWAY), my good friend
who serves on our Health Subcommittee and our Oversight and Investigations Subcommittee.
Mr. CONAWAY. Mr. Speaker, I rise
today in strong support of the Veterans’ Compensation Cost-of-Living
Adjustment Act.
Our veterans answered the call to
serve our country. They put their lives
on the line, made extraordinary sacrifices, and stood up to defend the freedoms we hold dear. At the very least,
we should do all that we can to ensure
that they and their families receive the
benefits they have earned and deserve.
As the cost of groceries, housing,
utilities, and everyday necessities continues to rise, we must make sure that
the benefits we provide veterans keep
pace with the cost of living.
This legislation does exactly that. It
aligns increases in veterans’ disability
compensation,
dependent
benefits,
clothing allowances, and survivor benefits with the annual cost-of-living adjustment provided to Social Security
recipients. That means that veterans
and their families will not be left behind as the cost of supporting a household continues to increase.
It is a matter of fairness. It is a matter of economic security. It is a matter
of keeping faith with those who have
kept their promises to our Nation.
Our commitment to veterans cannot
end when they take off the uniform. We
must continue to stand with them, support their families, and ensure they
have the resources and benefits they
deserve.
I urge my colleagues to support this
legislation.
Mr. HAMADEH of Arizona. Mr.

Members to support this legislation. I
yield back the balance of my time.

RECOGNIZING JEFF TECH
TRAINING PROGRAM
(Mr. THOMPSON of Pennsylvania
asked and was given permission to address the House for 1 minute and to revise and extend his remarks.)
Mr. THOMPSON. Mr. Speaker, I rise
today to recognize the new Jeff Tech
Farm to Refrigerator Training Program which was launched earlier this
year.
This innovative curriculum provides
educational opportunities for students
who are committed to strengthening
our country’s agriculture industry.
The program is a solution to the current shortage of meat processing professionals, and it will provide students
with hands-on experience and a strong
foundation in the science of meat cutting.
As the chairman of the House Committee on Agriculture, I am pleased to
see the advancements Jeff Tech is
making to ensure Pennsylvania producers have access to dependable meat
processors.
These students will support our supply chains and will keep beef and pork
upon our dinner tables. I commend the
school and all those who were involved
with planning this new curriculum.
This program is another example of
how Jeff Tech prepares its students for
high-demand jobs.
Mr. Speaker, as co-chair of the Career and Technical Education Caucus, I
am confident this curriculum will
strengthen our workforce and local
communities for years to come.
Mr. Speaker, I congratulate Jeff
Tech.

and guides us into the future, we seek
Your blessings upon the U.S. Senate

who will be leaving and those who will

2026 MIDTERM ELECTION

Mr. THUNE. Madam President, there
is no doubt about it, Tuesday night was
a tough election night. It was certainly

not the outcome that we had hoped for,
but it was the outcome the American
people chose, and we have to listen to
them.
I am proud of what Republicans have
been able to accomplish for the American people in the 119th Congress—
most especially, the Working Families
Tax Cuts, which allows hard-working
Americans to keep more of their hardearned money.
But the American people let us know
that they need more. Inflation is still
too high, and just going to the grocery
store can take a huge chunk out of a
family’s budget. And steep gas prices
have only increased that burden.
And so I think the election gave us
two things: one, an opportunity to reflect on what we as a party need to do
better; and, two, a clear message that
this coming Congress needs to double
down on the work that we have been
doing on affordability.
As I said, I am proud that this Republican Congress has put more money in
Americans’ pockets with the Working
Families Tax Cuts, and I am proud,
too, of other measures we passed, like
the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act,
which will help address the cost of
housing by increasing supply.
But as the American people have emphasized, there is more work to be
done. A very good start would be the
bipartisan permitting reform legislation that we will vote on this evening,
legislation that Republicans wanted to
bring up earlier this fall.
Energy prices affect pretty much everything when it comes to affordability. High energy costs don’t just
mean higher gas and electric bills.
They mean higher costs for a wide variety of goods and services, from hot
dogs to home repairs.
And so one of the biggest things that
we can do to address affordability for
the long term is to ensure a reliable
and affordable energy supply, and that
starts with ensuring that energy
projects don’t face unnecessary permitting barriers.

FLIGHT 5342 ACCIDENT

Mr. MORAN. Madam President,
sadly, on January 29, 2025, our Nation
witnessed a tragedy. We witnessed it
here in Washington, DC, at Reagan National Airport. Flight 5342, a regional
jet originating in Wichita, KS, collided
with a U.S. Army Black Hawk helicopter near that airport. Sixty-seven
people lost their lives. Seven of them
were from my State of Kansas.
Nearly 2 years later, their families
continue to live with an unimaginable
loss, and Congress still has not completed the comprehensive aviation
safety legislation necessary to address
the failures that contributed to the
tragedy. It is unacceptable.
Among those aboard Flight 5342 was
Grace Maxwell. Grace should have

PO 00000

Frm 00004

Fmt 4624

Sfmt 0634

graduated from Cedarville University
with her bachelor’s degree. And after
graduation, she planned to pursue a
master’s degree. Instead, her family is
left to imagine that future she would
have had. The Maxwell family is not
alone.
The families of the victims have continued to urge Congress to act, not
simply for their loved ones but to make
certain that no other family—no other
family—has to experience this kind of
tragedy. We owe them more than our
condolences. We owe them action.
In December, almost a year ago, the
Senate unanimously passed the bipartisan ROTOR Act to strengthen aviation safety and prevent future accidents.
The ROTOR Act was carefully developed with the support and input of the
crash victims’ families, the National
Transportation Safety Board, the Federal Aviation Administration, the Department of Transportation, and the
Department of Defense.
Rather than pass the Senate’s legislation, the House advanced its own proposal. The House bill contains important safety reforms. And I appreciate
the work of my colleagues in both
Chambers, but the two bills take different approaches to some of the important safety requirements. Productive negotiations have taken place between the House and Senate. I am encouraged by that progress, but we must
finish the job. We have been talking
about that progress and those negotiations for a long time. We must get the
job done. We must get it done right.
One of the most important provisions
in the ROTOR Act is the requirement
for Automatic Dependent SurveillanceBroadcast In, known as ADS-B In. This
technology provides pilots with realtime information about nearby aircraft. This allows pilots to see surrounding air traffic from their cockpits
and make better and quicker informed
decisions. It is particularly important
in congested airspace like the airspace
surrounding Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport.
Investigators from both the Army
and NTSB identified a series of failures
that contributed to the January 29
tragedy, including faulty equipment,
dangerous flightpaths, and inadequate
tracking technology. The NTSB concluded that the technology allowing pilots to see GPS-based information
about nearby aircraft could have
helped prevent this collision. With the
appropriate technology, pilots could
have had nearly a minute of warning to
recognize the danger and potentially
change the course—nearly a minute
that could have made the difference between the life and death of 67 people.
The ROTOR Act incorporates those
findings and puts critical safety improvements into law. It is not an arbitrary mandate. It is a recommendation
rooted in the independent investigation
of a tragedy that should never have
happened.
The House and Senate have different
approaches to ADS-B In. We need to

The PRESIDING OFFICER. The Senator from Rhode Island.
BIPARTISAN AMERICAN AFFORDABILITY AND
JOBS ACT OF 2026

Mr. WHITEHOUSE. Madam President, I am here a bit ahead of my colleague from the Environment and Public Works Committee, Chairman CAPITO, to say some words in favor of the
permitting reform bill that we are
about to consider moving to proceed.
In broad strokes, this is an affordability bill to begin with. For reasons
that are obvious to Rhode Islanders
who see offshore wind now beginning to
come ashore at 9 cents per kilowatt
hour into a grid that averages 18 cents
per kilowatt hour, the arrival of clean
energy as a supply is a very good thing
for ratepayers.
We, as we crafted this bill, had lots of
experts looking at it, and it is modeled
at this point to save American customers, ratepayers, more than $10 billion per year. So this is a real downpayment on the affordability agenda
that was so much at the front of Americans’ minds when they went to the
polls on Tuesday.
This gives us a chance to start now
with something that actually moves
quite quickly. This begins to generate
savings much more quickly than many
of the other issues that we are going to
have to deal with, like healthcare and
grocery prices and so forth. This is a
now savings as well as a real savings.
It is also the first bill to crack down
on data centers. It ends the data center
freeloading, period. Right now, a data
center can come to the grid, and it can
require the grid, the utility, to invest
tens of millions, hundreds of millions
of dollars in infrastructure for the massive load that it is about to dump onto
the grid. That all goes into the rate
base of the utility. That all becomes
the responsibility of all of the ratepayers. That is not fair. Our bill says
that ends. If you come to the grid with
a big, big demand, you have to pay for
the additional infrastructure that
needs to be added to meet your requirements.
By the way, that is a savings, too, because it is estimated that about $55 billion over 10 years that ratepayers
would have to pay for these data centers to come onto their grids—now that
goes to the data center developers
themselves. So if you are voting
against this bill, you are voting for a
$55 billion handout over 10 years to
data center developers. I don’t think
that is a good idea.
We have immense labor support for
this bill across the labor sector—the
Laborers’ International Union, Teamsters, IBEW, steelworkers, iron workers, plumbers and pipe fitters, operating engineers, boilermakers, building
trades—and that is because it is estimated to create over 100,000 jobs, and
those jobs are real jobs. Those are construction jobs on big projects where
people make great wages and in most
cases are union workers.
The last thing about it—I see that
my chairman is here, so I will wrap up.

UNANIMOUS CONSENT REQUEST—EXECUTIVE
CALENDAR

Mr. CRUZ. Mr. President, I rise today
to request confirmation of CDR Jesse
M. Millard to be captain in the U.S.
Coast Guard. His nomination was processed by the Commerce Committee
back in March of this year.
Commander Millard is a Coast Guard
Academy graduate with over 30 years
of Coast Guard service. Commander
Millard’s operational experience and
management responsibilities show that
he is well qualified for promotion. His
experience includes tours aboard medium endurance cutters, on intelligence assignment at Joint Interagency Task Force South, and senior
budgetary and logistics roles.
Commander Millard’s dedicated service has earned recognition from both
the Coast Guard and the Department of
Homeland Security. He has served on
two award-winning teams: the Coast
Guard’s Enterprise Budget Execution
Team, which received the 2022 Chief Financial Officer Award for Excellence,
and the Financial Resources Transition
Team, which received DHS’s 2022 David
Norquist Award for Excellence in Financial Management. These awards
recognize outstanding performance, innovative thinking, and superior mission achievements.
Commander Millard’s commitment
to the Coast Guard is shared by his
wife CDR Brooke Millard, who retired
from the Coast Guard in 2024 after 21
years of service. Brooke now serves as
the CEO of the Coast Guard’s official
family relief society, Coast Guard Mutual Assistance.
Promotions like this one are almost
always approved by the Senate unanimously, but not this time. Democrats
are attempting to kill Commander
Millard’s distinguished career over
false allegations perpetuated by a leftwing political activist who was known
throughout the Coast Guard for her
frequent complaints and inability to
get along with colleagues.
In October 2016, Commander Millard
completed an officer evaluation report
for this coworker. In his evaluation,
which recommended her for promotion,
Commander Millard described the officer as ‘‘competent, resourceful, and results-driven’’ and praised her ‘‘unwavering commitment to cadets.’’
Less than 3 months later, she was
promoted based in part on this evaluation, but she was nonetheless unhappy.
She had previously accused Commander Millard and his superiors of
having bullied her, in part because her
managers had rebuked her for being a
bad colleague when she unilaterally decided to repaint the staff’s office bright
orange.
After multiple complaints, including
complaints that she made to the Sec-

retary of DHS Alejandro Mayorkas, no

More than a year later, this individual filed a new complaint with the

coworker when he gave her a rating of

her 6’s and 7’s for the other categories.

from a 6 to a 5 because it was rare for
an officer not in a formal supervisory
role to receive a 6 in that category.

found that Commander Millard’s evaluation of the officer was retaliatory.

the subsequent Coast Guard review

First, as noted, Commander Millard’s
superiors agreed with the evaluation.

Indeed, a subsequent Coast Guard review Board even concluded that the
evaluation remarks Commander Millard provided were too high, the opposite of the IG’s conclusion that they
were too low.
Two separate Coast Guard Boards reviewed the inspector general’s report
and concluded that Millard should be
promoted. The most recent Board

Commander Millard’s colleagues submitted letters supporting him. One officer who served under Millard described him as ‘‘always extremely approachable and fair.’’ Those firsthand
assessments of his leadership deserve
serious consideration.

Commander Millard before. In 2018,
after the inspector general issued the

his promotion, this body confirmed
Commander Millard’s promotion to

cases is Commander Millard.

process can change the inspector general’s findings, which are supported by
the evidence.

Coast Guard to change.

those changes. I hope we can agree that
the Coast Guard going around an established process to move an individual
hurts the Coast Guard and the coastguardsmen who are serving our country.

Committee passed major structural reforms as part of a bipartisan Coast
Guard Reauthorization Act to address
those failures, and Congress must ensure that the right leadership is in
place to make those durable changes.
Promoting someone who engaged in
whistleblower retaliation, I don’t
think, would fulfill that mission.

BIPARTISAN AMERICAN
AFFORDABILITY AND JOBS ACT
Mr. VAN HOLLEN. Mr. President,
today I voted no on cloture on the motion to proceed to the Bipartisan
American Affordability and Jobs Act,
S. 5653. Permitting reform is needed to
fully unlock the clean energy transition—and the good-paying jobs and affordable energy that it will bring—and

VerDate Sep 11 2014

11:03 Nov 10, 2026

S5345

CONGRESSIONAL RECORD — SENATE

Jkt 079060

I appreciate the effort that has gone
into this bill. In reviewing it, I have focused on its potential to expand clean
and affordable energy and the need to
preserve critical protections for Maryland communities and the Chesapeake
Bay. As it stands, this bill falls short of
balancing those trade-offs, undercutting longstanding environmental protections without doing enough to protect the Maryland Offshore Wind
project from the Trump administration’s continued attacks.
The bill’s changes to the Clean Water
Act are particularly concerning, going
well beyond what is necessary to speed
up permitting of critical energy infrastructure and hamstringing Maryland’s
ability to effectively protect its waters
and the health of the Chesapeake Bay—
and may actually result in a two-tiered
State and Federal system that causes
additional delay. Language in the bill
on project certainty is meant to put a
stop to the Trump administration’s attacks on renewable energy projects,
but it fails to provide key protections
for Maryland’s Offshore Wind project—
the State’s largest renewable energy
project which would provide affordable,
reliable electricity to over 600,000
homes. Additionally, the bill’s limitations on judicial review go too far, especially to the National Historic Preservation Act and the National Environmental Policy Act, restricting the ability of communities to meaningfully
weigh in on projects that will impact
them.
We need permitting reform that
makes targeted changes to address real
problems while protecting the health of
communities and the environment. As
it currently stands, this bill needs
major improvements to meet that
mark. I will be introducing targeted
amendments to address my concerns
with the bill and will continue to push
for a robust amendment process to improve it.

The idea for The Goose began when

their shop as a place where locals could

enjoy life’s simple pleasures. To emphasize community even more, the
Merkles named the shop ‘‘The Goose,’’
symbolizing the tendency for geese to
fly together and lift each other up
along the way. The Goose opened in
July 2026. Following a successful summer season, Nickie and Rob expanded
the menu to include coffee to better
serve the community through the winter months.

a key role in Van Meter. Under Nickie
and Rob’s leadership, it has flourished
into a vibrant social hub that hosts
various community events. Their vision has become reality. To further engage with the community, The Goose
partnered with a local elementary
school to showcase student designs on
its coffee cup sleeves and in the ’’Goose
Gallery’’ on the store’s walls. The shop
also stays open late after large community events like high school homecoming and Music in The Park, so
locals can grab a bite. The Goose
sources its ice cream from Hiland
Dairy and offers customers a wide
range of flavors. The coffee menu features lattes, cold brew, and specialty
drinks. Both coffee and ice cream orders can be placed online or in-store.

the success of The Goose to the community and staff who have supported
them along the way.

Business and Entrepreneurship, each

Natural Fertilizer of Harrison County,

Abe Sandquist came up with the idea
of Natural Fertilizer after spending
several years developing nutrient management plans for the USDA. His time
there revealed that many agricultural
producers did not realize the value of
organic nutrients until they received
professional guidance on how to effectively use them. Seeing the strong demand for assistance, Abe established
Natural Fertilizer in 2007 to provide
nutrient management consulting services. Since then, Natural Fertilizer has
continued to grow. In 2009, Abe recognized the potential in brokering and
selling excess manure to neighboring
farms. Abe’s decision to enter this new
field allowed Natural Fertilizer to
partner with local manure haulers,
transforming the business into a fullservice operation that incorporated
transporting, marketing, and fertilizing. In 2021, Natural Fertilizer acquired Soil Solutions in Onawa, IA.
This allowed the business to recycle industrial byproducts into high-value fertilizers and expand its reach to farmers
in other States.
Today, Natural Fertilizer mainly focuses on the nutrient cycle of organic
residuals in addition to its consulting
services. Abe’s goal is for everyone to
win: the community, the processors,
the feedlots, and the farmers. Abe and
his team of 30 employees and 30 contractors have expanded operations to
include two recycling centers in western Iowa. At these processing plants,
heat and microbes break down thousands of tons of organic matter, transforming the waste into nutrient-rich,
sustainable, and affordable fertilizer.
Once fully processed and tested for
quality, the business distributes its fertilizer to over 500 farmers across Iowa.
In 2025, Abe was awarded the USDA
Fertilizer Production Expansion Program, FPEP, grant to begin constructing the Waste Into Nutrient Recovery, WINR Center. Since then, construction of a second WINR Center has
begun, and a site for a third has been
purchased. Abe hopes that Natural Fertilizer will one day be the national
standard.
Natural
Fertilizer’s
impressive
growth has been recognized by several
organizations in the community. The
Harrison County Farm Bureau honored
Abe with the 2026 Distinguished Service to Agriculture Award. In 2025,
Iowa’s Small Business Development
Center awarded him the Neal Smith
Entrepreneur of the Year Award for
Sustainable Innovation in Agricultural
Waste. That same year, Abe was named
Iowa Entrepreneur of the Year. Beyond
these accolades, Abe remains an active
member of Woodbine Iowa’s IGNITE
Pathways Program, which provides

TRIBUTE TO VAN INGRAM
∑ Mr. MCCONNELL. Mr. President, I
would like to take a moment to honor
Van Ingram, the executive director of
the Kentucky Office of Drug Control
Policy, ODCP, who is retiring at the
end of this year after 22 years as one of
the Commonwealth’s leading drug enforcement officers. I have worked
closely with Van to combat the issues
of substance abuse, addiction, and the
opioid crisis that has plagued our
state. It is my privilege to look back at
Van’s lengthy career in public service
fighting for the betterment of the people of the great State of Kentucky.
Prior to joining the Kentucky Office
of Drug Control Policy, Van spent
more than 23 years in the Maysville
Police Department, including his final
6 as chief. In 2001, Van was named Kentucky Chief of the Year and received
the Governor’s Award for Outstanding
Contribution to Law Enforcement in
2004, the same year that the ODCP was
created. The ODCP’s office’s main mission since its inception when it was
formed has been to help communities
throughout the Commonwealth understand substance abuse and reduce the
risk of addiction, while coordinating
efforts with law enforcement and other
agencies to help those receive the
treatment and help they need. Van was
at the forefront of these efforts and became executive director of the office in
2009. Van led drug-control policy in
Kentucky during a time when the
State was at in the height of its struggle with the opioid crisis. In 2012, Van
helped Kentucky strengthen its prescription-monitoring efforts by requiring many prescribers to check the Kentucky All Schedule Prescription Electronic Reporting system, known as
KASPER, before prescribing controlled
substances. Thanks to Van’s innovation and leadership, almost all States
in the years since have established
similar systems.
During my time as Senate leader, I
was proud to leverage my leadership
role and work alongside Van in fighting the substance abuse epidemic.

E:\CR\FM\A09NO6.019

S09NOPT1

S5348

From 2000–2012, Kentucky saw hospitalizations
for
drug-dependent
newborns drastically increase from 28
in 2000 to 824 in 2012. By 2018, the crisis
had worsened, with Kentucky ranking
fifth for the most overdose deaths in
the Nation. Van and I both shared a
commitment to finding solutions to

new legislative efforts and created new
programs to help combat the epidemic,

drug overdose deaths since 1990.
