REMEMBERING DAVID HOLLISTER
∑ Ms. SLOTKIN. Mr. President, it is
my honor to recognize the life and public service of the late David C. Hollister, the esteemed former mayor of
Lansing, MI.
Mr. Hollister passed away earlier this
year at the age of 84, leaving behind a
remarkable career of passionate public
service to Michigan. He transformed
our State for the better, especially our
capital
city,
for
generations
of
Michiganders.
Born in Kalamazoo in 1942 and raised
in Battle Creek, Mr. Hollister studied
at Kellogg Community College and
Michigan State University. While
studying at MSU, he was inspired by a
speech Rev. Martin Luther King, Jr.,
gave, as well as a chance meeting with
him. This compelled Mr. Hollister to
travel to Mississippi to volunteer as a
teacher on the frontlines of the civil
rights movement. These life-changing
experiences encouraged him toward
public service.
A common thread throughout Mr.
Hollister’s life was his commitment to
peace, social justice, equality, education, and human rights. His philosophy was called ‘‘VP3.’’ First, you need
a positive vision to help people. Then,
you need the three ‘‘Ps’’: a plan to get
there, partners who are truly committed to the vision, and perseverance
to get it done. This was the foundation
of his five decades of public service,
which were marked by integrity, consistency, and passion for a better
Michigan.
Mr. Hollister first served Michigan as
a teacher in Durand and Lansing. He
saw firsthand how many of his students
suffered because they did not have
enough food at home or their families
could not pay their bills. These experiences drove him to run for elected office. He served on the Ingham County
Board of Commissioners and then nearly two decades in the Michigan House
of Representatives. Chairing the appropriations subcommittee on social services for one decade, Mr. Hollister was a
staunch advocate for helping families
get the healthcare, food, wages, and resources they needed to stay healthy.

PO 00000

Frm 00013

Fmt 4624

Sfmt 0634

He helped establish the Greater Lansing Food Alliance, now known as the
Greater Lansing Food Bank, a lifeline
providing food to families in need.
Mr. Hollister is most revered for his
leadership in revitalizing Lansing into
the incredible city that Michiganders
enjoy and love today. He believed to
his core that Lansing was the best city
in the world. When he spoke about his
positive vision for the city, he was passionate and excited; and Lansing elected him three times as mayor to carry
it out, starting in 1993.
When you drive down Michigan Avenue, you see a beautiful baseball stadium and a sea of restaurants, shops,
and apartments. Much of that is because of Mr. Hollister. He helped establish the beloved Lansing Lugnuts, a
minor league baseball team that helped
revitalize Lansing’s downtown.
He also helped strengthen Lansing’s
economy. When General Motors announced plans in 1996 to close plants in
the region, Mr. Hollister created a
grassroots coalition of labor unions,
business leaders, State officials, and
community advocates from both sides
of the aisle to keep the business in
town. Their efforts were successful,
saving thousands of good-paying jobs
and ensuring Lansing’s economy was
set up for success for decades to come.
He also helped bring new industries to
the region that are still thriving today.
For his tenacious and strong-willed
service to Lansing, the capital’s city
hall now bears his name. Mr. Hollister
also served at Michigan State University and as the director of the Michigan Department of Labor and Economic Growth under former Gov. Jennifer Granholm.
Mr. Hollister was a champion for
Lansing who will be dearly missed by
our State. He was also a proud and caring husband, father, grandfather,
friend, and mentor.
As we celebrate David Hollister’s life,
it is my honor to appreciate his lifetime of getting things done to help
Michigan families and children, especially in our State’s wonderful capital
city.∑

TRIBUTE TO BRYAN PRICE
∑ Mr. YOUNG. Mr. President, I rise
today to recognize Bryan Price, who
will retire from his role as the president and CEO of the Indiana University
Credit Union in April 2027.
Bryan has been with IU Credit Union
for more than 40 years, spending the
last 20 as its president and CEO.
Throughout his career, Bryan has provided leadership that has benefited the
credit union’s 72,000 members, touching
communities throughout the State. In
addition to his contributions to the IU
Credit Union, Bryan worked on behalf
of Indiana’s more than 2.8 million credit union members through service on
the board of Indiana’s Department of
Financial Institutions, the Consumer
Financial Protection Bureau Credit
Union Advisory Council, the Chicago
Federal Reserve Bank Community Depository Institution Advisory Council,
and the board of the Indiana Credit
Union League.
Bryan has provided leadership with
exceptional vision, integrity, and an
unwavering commitment to improving
the financial well-being of Indiana families and communities. Under his stewardship, IU Credit Union has grown
into one of Indiana’s largest and most
respected credit unions while remaining steadfast in its cooperative, member-focused mission. He has consistently championed the belief that a
credit union’s purpose extends beyond
banking: that it exists to strengthen
the community it serves. His leadership has inspired employees, community partners, and fellow credit union
leaders to embrace that same philosophy of service.
His leadership has fostered a culture
of service and community investment

PO 00000

Frm 00014

Fmt 4624

Sfmt 0634

that has produced meaningful and lasting benefits for Hoosiers. This has included the credit union contributing
more than $300,000 annually to community sponsorships and charitable initiatives; awarding more than $47,000 annually in scholarships to students pursuing higher education; supporting
United Way campaigns, affordable
housing initiatives, financial literacy
programs, and numerous nonprofit organizations throughout south-central
Indiana; and investing in partnerships
that improve educational opportunities, economic development, and the
overall quality of life for Hoosier communities.
Bryan has also distinguished himself
as one of Indiana’s most effective credit union advocates. He has worked with
legislators and regulators at the State
and Federal levels to help shape public
policy and improve consumer access to
affordable financial services. In recognition of these accomplishments and
more, he was inducted into the Indiana
Credit Union Hall of Fame on October
2 of this year.
Bryan’s legacy will be measured not
only by the growth and success of the
organizations he led; it will also be
measured by the countless lives he has
positively impacted through his commitment to public service, financial
empowerment, education, and community investment. He embodies the leadership qualities that others look up to,
and his contributions have left a lasting mark on his credit union, community, colleagues, and everyone who
benefited because of his dedication to
the cooperative principle of people
helping people.∑

STATEMENTS ON INTRODUCED
BILLS AND JOINT RESOLUTIONS
By Mr. PADILLA (for himself and
Mr. SCHIFF):
S. 5694. A bill to take certain land in
the State of California into trust for
the benefit of the Barona Group of Capitan Grande Band of Mission Indians
of the Barona Reservation, California,
and for other purposes; to the Committee on Indian Affairs.
Mr. PADILLA. Mr. President, I rise
today to introduce a bill to transfer a
total of 847 acres of Federal land in San
Diego County, CA, currently administered by the Bureau of Land Management, BLM, and the U.S. Forest Service, USFS, to be held in trust for the
Barona Band Mission Indians.
The transfer of these three parcels
would unify the Tribe with their ancestral home, which has since been fragmented, to allow for land management
consistent with the Tribe’s cultural
traditions and practices. The Tribe has
also worked with BLM and USFS to
preserve existing rights-of-way, public
recreational access and public trails,
emergency access for Federal personnel, and existing water rights and
service agreements.
The Tribe was forced out of their
first federally established reservation
when the city of San Diego bought a
portion of the Capitan Grande Reservation from the Federal Government to
build a reservoir. After the reservation
was flooded, the Tribe purchased the
Barona property in 1932 to create their
current reservation. The Barona Tribe
and the Viejas Band of Kumeyaay Indians now share a joint-trust patent to
jointly manage the remaining 15,000
acres of the Capitan Grande Reservation surrounding the reservoir.
The proposed parcels in this bill are
adjacent to the existing 7,500 acre
Barona Indian Reservation near Ramona and have deep cultural and historical significance to the Tribe. Adding this land into trust would act as a
bridge—connecting the land between
the Barona Indian Reservation and the
Capitan Grande Reservation. This legislation would allow the Tribe to better
protect sacred sites, traditional use
areas, and cultural resources on ancestral land.
I want to thank Senator SCHIFF for
cosponsoring this legislation and Rep-

Whereas, across the United States, clean
and readily abundant forms of energy are
powering more homes and businesses than

Whereas clean energy generation is readily
available from zero- and low-emissions

has been a key driver of economic growth in
the United States;
Whereas technological innovation can further reduce costs, enhance reliability, and
increase deployment of clean energy sources;
Whereas the report of the Department of
Energy entitled ‘‘2025 U.S. Energy & Employment Report’’ found that, at the end of 2024,
the energy and energy efficiency sectors in

Whereas the scaling of affordable and exportable clean energy is essential to reducing global emissions;

and clean energy jobs are part of the energy

S. RES. 951
Whereas the term ‘‘infant mortality’’ refers to the death of a baby before the first
birthday of the baby;
Whereas, each year, approximately 20,000
infants in the United States die in the first
year of life;
Whereas the United States ranks 32nd out
of the 38 countries in the Organisation for
Economic Co-operation and Development
(referred to in this preamble as ‘‘OECD’’) for
infant mortality rate, with 5.5 deaths per
1,000 live births;
Whereas high rates of infant mortality are
especially prevalent in minority and underserved communities, including communities
experiencing high rates of poverty and unemployment and those with limited access to
health care providers;
Whereas more than 35 percent of counties
are considered maternity care deserts, where
there is no access to birthing hospitals, birth
centers offering obstetric care, or obstetric
providers, affecting more than 2,300,000
women of reproductive age and impacting
150,000 births in 2022;
Whereas approximately half of rural communities lack a birthing facility or obstetrician;
Whereas the leading causes of infant mortality are—
(1) birth defects;
(2) low birth weight;
(3) sudden infant death syndrome;
(4) unintentional injuries;
(5) maternal complications;
(6) bacterial sepsis of newborn; and
(7) cord and placental complications;
Whereas infant mortality can be substantially reduced through—
(1) community-based services, such as outreach, home visitation, care coordination,
health education, and interconceptional
care;
(2) early prenatal care; and
(3) paternal involvement;
Whereas support for community-based programs to reduce infant mortality may result
in lower spending on medical interventions,
special education, and other social services
required by infants and children born with a
low birth weight;
Whereas the Department of Health and
Human Services has implemented the Newborn Supply Kit program;
Whereas newborn screening is important to
detecting potentially fatal or disabling conditions as early as possible, often before the
infant displays any signs or symptoms of a
disease or condition, and early detection allows treatment to begin immediately, which
may lead to eliminate or reduce the effects
of the condition;
Whereas, if left untreated, these conditions
can have serious effects, such as lifelong
nervous system damage, intellectual, developmental, and physical disabilities, and even
death;
Whereas untreated maternal mental health
conditions during pregnancy have been
linked to adverse birth outcomes, including
preterm birth and low birth weight babies,
which can impact infant mortality;

Whereas the Philip A. Hart Senate Office

‘‘Hart Building’’) is home to Alexander

Whereas Alexander Calder’s Mountains and
Clouds was commissioned for the Hart Building and conceived as an integral part of the
building’s architecture and public spaces;
Whereas Alexander Calder’s design was selected by the Architect of the Capitol in 1975
and the plans were presented in November
1976, with installation completed in November 1986;
Whereas Alexander Calder (1898-1976) was
one of America’s greatest sculptors of the
20th century, known for his invention of the
suspended moving sculpture, with Mountains
and Clouds representing his final work;

SENATE
CONCURRENT
RESOLUTION 41—RECOGNIZING THE SIGNIFICANCE OF EQUAL PAY AND
THE DISPARITY IN WAGES PAID
TO LATINAS IN COMPARISON TO
WHITE, NON-HISPANIC MEN
Ms. CORTEZ MASTO submitted the
following concurrent resolution; which
was referred to the Committee on
Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions:
Whereas October 8, 2026, is designated as
‘‘Latina Equal Pay Day’’ to observe the pay
gap between Latinas and White, non-Hispanic men;
Whereas, as of 2025, there were 15,276,000
Hispanic women in the labor force, representing approximately 17 percent of all
women in the labor force;
Whereas section 6(d) of the Fair Labor
Standards Act of 1938 (29 U.S.C. 206(d)) (commonly known as the ‘‘Equal Pay Act of
1963’’) prohibits discrimination in wages on
the basis of sex for equal work;
Whereas title VII of the Civil Rights Act of
1964 (42 U.S.C. 2000e et seq.) prohibits discrimination in compensation because of
race, color, religion, national origin, or sex;
Whereas, despite the passage of the Equal
Pay Act of 1963 (Public Law 88–38; 77 Stat. 56)
more than 6 decades ago, which established
that employers shall not discriminate in
wages on the basis of sex but shall provide
equal pay for equal work, Bureau of the Census data show that Latinas working fulltime and year-round are paid 60 cents for
every dollar paid to White, non-Hispanic
men, while the average wage differential for
all Latinas with reported earnings working
full-time, part-time, and part-year is 53 cents
for every dollar paid to White, non-Hispanic
men;
Whereas an analysis by Justice for Migrant
Women shows that Latinas in rural communities are paid, on average, 43 cents for every
dollar made by White, non-Hispanic men and
face unique challenges that contribute to the

PO 00000

Frm 00023

Fmt 4624

Sfmt 0634

pay gap, including lack of access to transportation, child care, and health care;
Whereas National Latina Equal Pay Day is
vital to acknowledge and understand the
economic reality of Latinas and the impact
that their race, gender identity, occupation,
migration status, and geographic location
have on their earnings;
Whereas
increased
and
further
disaggregated data is necessary to understand the impact of the pay gap within different groups of women of the same racial or
ethnic background;
Whereas the pay gap for Latinas persists
across sectors and education levels;
Whereas an analysis by the National Partnership for Women & Families of data from
the Bureau of the Census shows that disabled
Latinas are paid 46 cents for every dollar
paid to White, non-Hispanic, nondisabled
men;
Whereas the National Women’s Law Center
has calculated that, on average, Latinas lose
over $1,344,800 in potential earnings over a
40-year career to the wage gap;
Whereas lost wages due to the wage gap
mean Latinas have less money to support
themselves and their families, save and invest for the future, and spend on goods and
services;
Whereas the lack of access to affordable,
quality child care, paid family and medical
leave, and other family-friendly workplace
policies forces many Latinas to choose between their paycheck or job and getting
quality care for themselves or their family
members, a dynamic that contributes to the
wage gap;
Whereas workplace harassment forces
many women to leave their occupation or industry, or pass up opportunities for advancement, which contributes to the gender wage
gap;
Whereas targets of workplace harassment
are 6.5 times as likely as nontargets to
change jobs;
Whereas there is a high personal cost for
women who have been sexually harassed, including unemployment, under-employment,
and financial stress resulting from changing
jobs, which leads to long-term consequences
for earnings and career attainment;
Whereas, in 2025, more than 61 percent of
the low-paid workforce were women;
Whereas the pay disparity Latinas face is
part of a wider set of disparities Latinas face
in homeownership, unemployment, poverty,
access to childcare, and the ability to build
wealth;
Whereas the underpayment of Latina
workers causes businesses and the economy
to suffer;
Whereas true pay equity requires a multifaceted strategy that addresses the gender
and racial injustices that Latinas face daily;
and
Whereas many national organizations have
designated October 8, 2026, as ‘‘Latina Equal
Pay Day’’ to recognize the pay gap between
Latinas and White, non-Hispanic men in the
prior year: Now, therefore, be it
Resolved by the Senate (the House of Representatives concurring), That Congress—
(1) recognizes the disparity in wages paid
to Latinas and the impact of that disparity
on women, families, the economy, and the
United States; and

Mr. CRUZ. Mr. President, I ask unanimous consent that the Senate proceed

to the immediate consideration of Calendar No. 543, S. 3589.
The PRESIDING OFFICER.
clerk will report the bill by title.

The

The senior assistant legislative clerk
read as follows:
A bill (S. 3589) to amend the Higher Education Act of 1965 to provide students with
disabilities and their families with access to
critical information needed to select the
right college and succeed once enrolled.

There being no objection, the Senate
proceeded to consider the bill, which
had been reported from the Committee
on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions with an amendment to strike all
after the enacting clause and insert in
lieu thereof the following:

PO 00000

Frm 00040

Fmt 4624

Sfmt 6333

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.

This Act may be cited as the ‘‘Respond, Innovate, Succeed, and Empower Act’’ or the ‘‘RISE
Act’’.
SEC. 2. PERFECTING AMENDMENT TO THE DEFINITION OF DISABILITY.

Section 103(6) of the Higher Education Act of
1965 (20 U.S.C. 1003(6)) is amended by striking
‘‘section 3(2)’’ and inserting ‘‘section 3’’.
SEC. 3. SUPPORTING STUDENTS WITH DISABILITIES TO SUCCEED ONCE ENROLLED
IN COLLEGE.

Section 487(a) of the Higher Education Act of
1965 (20 U.S.C. 1094(a)) is amended by adding at
the end the following:
‘‘(30)(A) The institution will carry out the following:
‘‘(i) Adopt policies that make any of the following documentation submitted by an individual sufficient to establish that such individual is an individual with a disability:

E:\CR\FM\A09NO6.021

S09NOPT1

November 9, 2026

‘‘(I) Documentation that the individual has
had an individualized education program (referred to in this paragraph as an ‘IEP’) in accordance with section 614(d) of the Individuals
with Disabilities Education Act, if the IEP for
the student was utilized at any point in high
school (without regard as to whether the date of
the student’s most recent evaluation or reevaluation occurred before the student entered high
school).
‘‘(II) Documentation describing services or accommodations provided to the individual pursuant to section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of
1973 (29 U.S.C. 794) (referred to in this paragraph as a ‘Section 504 plan’), if the Section 504
plan for the student was utilized at any point in
high school (without regard as to whether the
date of the student’s most recent evaluation or
reevaluation occurred before the student entered
high school).
‘‘(III) A plan or record of service for the individual from a private high school, a local educational agency, a State educational agency, or
an institution of higher education provided in
accordance with the Americans with Disabilities
Act of 1990 (42 U.S.C. 12101 et seq.).
‘‘(IV) A record or evaluation from a relevant
licensed professional finding that the individual
has a disability.
‘‘(V) A plan or record of disability from another institution of higher education.
‘‘(VI) Documentation of a disability due to
service in the uniformed services, as defined in
section 484C(a).
‘‘(ii) Adopt policies that are transparent and
explicit regarding information about the process
by which the institution determines eligibility
for reasonable accommodations or modifications
consistent with section 504 of the Rehabilitation
Act of 1973 (29 U.S.C. 794) and the Americans
with Disabilities Act of 1990 (42 U.S.C. 12101 et
seq.).
‘‘(iii) Disseminate such information to students, parents, and faculty in an accessible format, including during any student orientation
and making such information readily available
on a public website of the institution.
‘‘(B) Nothing in this paragraph shall be construed to preclude an institution from establishing less burdensome criteria than that described in subparagraph (A) to establish an individual as an individual with a disability who
may be eligible for reasonable accommodations
or modifications.’’.
SEC. 4. AUTHORIZATION OF FUNDS FOR THE NATIONAL CENTER FOR INFORMATION
AND TECHNICAL SUPPORT FOR
POSTSECONDARY STUDENTS WITH
DISABILITIES.

Section 777(a) of the Higher Education Act of
1965 (20 U.S.C. 1140q(a)) is amended—
(1) in paragraph (1), by striking ‘‘From
amounts appropriated under section 778,’’ and
inserting ‘‘From amounts appropriated under
paragraph (5),’’; and
(2) by adding at the end the following:
‘‘(5) AUTHORIZATION OF APPROPRIATIONS.—
There is authorized to be appropriated to carry
out this subsection $10,000,000 for the period of
fiscal years 2027 through 2031.’’.

dmwilson on DSK7X7S144PROD with SENATE

SEC. 5. INCLUSION OF INFORMATION ON STUDENTS WITH DISABILITIES.
(a) IN GENERAL.—Section 487(a) of the Higher

Education Act of 1965 (20 U.S.C. 1094(a)), as
amended by section 3, is further amended—
(1) by redesignating paragraphs (18) through
(30) as paragraphs (19) through (31), respectively; and
(2) by inserting after paragraph (17) the following:
‘‘(18)(A) The institution will submit, for inclusion in the Integrated Postsecondary Education
Data System (IPEDS) or any other Federal postsecondary institution data collection effort, key
data related to undergraduate and graduate
students enrolled in the institution who are formally registered as students with disabilities
with the institution’s office of disability services

VerDate Sep 11 2014

11:03 Nov 10, 2026

S5377

CONGRESSIONAL RECORD — SENATE

Jkt 079060

(which, for purposes of this paragraph, includes
an equivalent office), including—
‘‘(i) the total number of undergraduate and
graduate students registered with the institution’s office of disability services;
‘‘(ii) the number of undergraduate and graduate students accessing or receiving reasonable
accommodations or modifications, as voluntarily
reported to the institution’s office of disability
services;
‘‘(iii) the percentage of undergraduate and
graduate students enrolled in the institution
who are registered with the institution’s office
of disability services; and
‘‘(iv) the total number of undergraduate and
graduate certificates or degrees awarded to students registered with the institution’s office of
disability services.
‘‘(B) Notwithstanding subparagraph (A), an
institution shall not be required to submit information under this paragraph if the number of
such students would reveal personally identifiable information about an individual student.’’.
(b) CONFORMING AMENDMENTS.—
(1) HIGHER EDUCATION ACT OF 1965.—The Higher Education Act of 1965 (20 U.S.C. 1001 et seq.)
is amended—
(A) in the matter preceding clause (i) of section 152(a)(1)(A) (20 U.S.C. 1019a(a)(1)(A)), by
striking ‘‘(a)(27)’’ and inserting ‘‘(a)(28)’’;
(B) in section 153(c)(3) (20 U.S.C. 1019b(c)(3)),
by striking ‘‘section 487(a)(25)’’ each place the

and
(C) in section 487 (20 U.S.C. 1094)—
(i) in subsection (d), by striking ‘‘subsection
(a)(24)’’ each place the term appears and inserting ‘‘subsection (a)(25)’’;
(ii) in the matter preceding paragraph (1) of
subsection (e), by striking ‘‘subsection (a)(25)’’
and inserting ‘‘subsection (a)(26)’’; and
(iii) in the matter preceding subparagraph (A)
of subsection (h)(1), by striking ‘‘subsection
(a)(27)’’ and inserting ‘‘subsection (a)(28)’’.
(2) TITLE 38, UNITED STATES CODE.—Title 38,
United States Code, is amended—
(A) in section 3679(f)(2)(C), by striking ‘‘section 487(a)(20) of the Higher Education Act of
1965 (20 U.S.C. 1094(a)(20))’’ and inserting ‘‘section 487(a)(21) of the Higher Education Act of
1965 (20 U.S.C. 1094(a)(21))’’; and
(B) in section 3696(c)(2), by striking ‘‘section
487(a)(20) of the Higher Education Act of 1965
(20 U.S.C. 1094(a)(20))’’ and inserting ‘‘section
487(a)(21) of the Higher Education Act of 1965
(20 U.S.C. 1094(a)(21))’’.
SEC. 6. RULES OF CONSTRUCTION.

None of the amendments made by this Act
shall be construed to affect—
(1) the meanings of the terms ‘‘reasonable accommodation’’, ‘‘reasonable modification’’, and
‘‘record of impairment’’ under the Americans
with Disabilities Act of 1990 (42 U.S.C. 12101 et
seq.) or section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of
1973 (29 U.S.C. 794); or
(2) the rights or remedies provided under such
Acts.

been an integral part of the local community
since its establishment and continues to uphold its mission to provide residents with community betterment and support.

movement for vision and blindness prevention
following Helen Keller’s influential 1925 address. This organization’s first event debuted
at Bahrs Landing and drew over 100
attendees, including Lions District Governor
Carl Banwart. The night featured speeches,
musical performances, and installation of the
original officer slate. From the 1930s to the
1950s, recurring fundraising events and
themed social gatherings formed lasting community traditions. Today, the Highlands Lions
Club continues to have a special social, recreational, and charitable presence in Highlands.

CELEBRATING THE HONORABLE

LOUISIANA POLITICAL HALL OF

HON. TROY A. CARTER
OF LOUISIANA

IN THE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES

Monday, November 9, 2026
Mr. CARTER of Louisiana. Mr. Speaker, I
rise today to honor an incredible man, the person that launched my political career upon my
graduation from Xavier University of Louisiana,
the Honorable Sidney J. Barthelemy, New Orleans’ 58th Mayor of the City of New Orleans
from 1986 to 1994. The second African American to hold the New Orleans mayoral chair,
he was a member of the Louisiana State Senate from 1974 to 1978 and a member at-large

CONGRESSIONAL RECORD — Extensions of Remarks

of the New Orleans City Council from 1978 to
1986. He is a proud, dedicated member of the
Democratic Party.
The Honorable Barthelemy dedicated his life
to public service and civic leadership, guided
by a belief that government should serve all
people. A lifelong resident of New Orleans,
Barthelemy’s career reflects a deep commitment to community, equity, and responsible
governance.
Barthelemy graduated from St. Augustine
High School, earned a B.A. in philosophy from
the St. Joseph Seminary in Washington, D.C.,
and later a Master of Social Work from Tulane
University. Before entering politics, he worked
as a social worker and community advocate,
experiences that shaped his compassionate
and practical approach to leadership.
In 1974, Barthelemy began his political career, winning a seat in the Louisiana State
Senate. His election was historic, as he became the first African American to serve in the
Louisiana State Senate since the Reconstruction era. In 1978, he won his first city-wide
election and served two terms as Councilmanat-Large. During his tenure, he earned a reputation as a thoughtful policymaker with strong
oversight of municipal finances, public utilities,
and neighborhood development. His service
on key committees provided him with a deep
understanding of city operations and laid the
foundation for higher office.
In 1986. Barthelemy was elected Mayor of
New Orleans, becoming the city’s second African American mayor. Serving two terms, he
led the city through a period of economic and
infrastructural transition. His administration
emphasized fiscal responsibility, economic development, tourism, and downtown revitalization, helping strengthen New Orleans’ national
profile while maintaining stability during challenging times.
Known for his calm demeanor and collaborative leadership style, Barthelemy sought to
bridge communities and represent all citizens.
Following his time as mayor, he remained active in civic and cultural affairs. Married to
Michaele Barthelemy for 57 years, they have
3 children, Cherrie, Bridget, and Sidney, II.
I credit my role as a Member of Congress
today, because of the opportunities and guidance I received from the Honorable Sidney
Barthelemy. I thank the The Louisiana Political
Museum and Hall of Fame Foundation for assuring his legacy continues.

paramedic, instructor, and special operations
team member, Armando Jose Rivas Herrera
has dedicated his professional life to ensuring
that first responders are better prepared, more
capable, and safer when responding to emergencies.
He began his service in Caracas, Venezuela, where he worked as an emergency
nurse, paramedic, disaster-response professional, and instructor. These experiences
shaped his commitment to training, leadership,
and the belief that preparation saves lives.
Today, Armando serves in Florida’s fire
service, where he actively supports fire suppression, emergency medical services, special
operations, and firefighter development. As an
instructor and Field Training Officer, he has
helped prepare countless firefighters to respond effectively in high-risk environments.
His commitment to excellence was recognized
when he was named Fire Instructor of the
Year for 2025.
In 2022, Armando founded Fire Rescue
Group, an organization dedicated to expanding access to high-quality firefighter training
and emergency-response education. Through
this effort, he has provided instruction, consulting, and mentorship to firefighters and
emergency-response organizations across the
United States and numerous countries around
the world, fostering international collaboration
and the exchange of lifesaving knowledge.
Armando has also demonstrated a deep
commitment to humanitarian service, helping
coordinate support and emergency resources
for first responders affected by the 2026 earthquake in Venezuela.

Mr. CARTER of Louisiana. Mr. Speaker, I
rise today to celebrate the life of New Orleans’

November 9, 2026

beloved native son, William ‘‘Bill’’ Rouselle,
Jr., a true friend, mentor and confidant to
many, and most notably, a Civil Rights Pioneer, William ‘‘Bill’’ Rouselle, Jr., was a native
and proud New Orleanian who broke barriers
and changed the lives of countless people
through his motto of ‘‘Speak Truth to the People,’’ and fought a fight grounded in hope and
optimism for equity among all people.
On Sunday, July 21, 2026, he went home to
receive his crown. Faithful to the end, he
leaves a legacy that endures based on Proverbs 3:5–6, ‘‘Trust in the Lord, with all thine
heart. And lean not unto thine own understanding. In all thy ways, acknowledge Him,
and He shall direct thy path.’’
Born in New Orleans on August 3, 1946, his
life in the media is rooted in a desire for the
truth, a commitment to change, and a will to
leave this world a better place. He was preceded in death by his parents, Edmonia Nelson and William Rouselle, Sr. The son of a
public-school teacher, Bill grew up in Uptown
New Orleans. Nurtured by the rich New Orleans culture, he developed a love for his city,
its people. He attended Xavier University Preparatory School and was a 1967 Honors
Graduate from Xavier University of Louisiana.
Following graduation, Rouselle landed a
publishing intern position with Time, Inc. in
New York. That next year, he became the first
African American on-air news reporter in New
Orleans at WDSU TV. Rouselle often shares
his first day in the WDSU newsroom, April 4,
1968—the day Martin Luther King was assassinated. He saw first-hand how media censorship works when police authorities convinced
the TV station not to air information on the
riots in other urban areas in America. They
feared similar reactions from local citizens. His
passion for truth and commitment to his people grew stronger.
In 1969, he left WDSU following a controversial interview with the protesters who
were fighting the merger of SUNO into the
LSU System. He would be appointed as Deputy Director of the City’s Human Relations
Committee where he engineered the passage
of a local Public Accommodations Ordinance,
opening restaurants and bars to all citizens.
Following a year at City Hall, he worked ten
years in the community with the Free Southern Theater (FST). He helped organize a community-based effort to include African Americans in the TV media. The Media Project challenged TV stations’ licenses in the early 1970s
and won concessions from most of the local
TV stations. In the mid-1970s, Bill hosted a
weekly TV show on the public television station WYES TV called Nation Time while also
serving as Producer for the Free Southern
Theater. During this period, Rouselle joined
the board of the New Orleans Jazz and Heritage Foundation following a protest for Black
involvement in the event. He would eventually
serve as president and help oversee the development of the festival into one of the
world’s premier music events.
Rouselle later worked as director of the Parent Community Alliance, an organization that
was developed to encourage parents to be
more involved in public school policy. He
learned about community organizing in this
role under the tutelage of Oretha Castle
Haley, his most important mentor. In the late
1970s, Bill headed the Ad Hoc Committee for
Accountable Police, which won increased civilian oversight of police involved in brutal citizen
interactions.

VerDate Sep 11 2014

08:40 Nov 10, 2026

E1167

CONGRESSIONAL RECORD — Extensions of Remarks

Jkt 079060

In the early 1980s, Rouselle put his publishing skills to work at the Black Collegian
Magazine, a Black-owned and operated national publication based in New Orleans. Then,
in 1984, he and former Black Collegian editor
Kalamu ya Salaam opened the doors of Bright
Moments Public Relations firm servicing a
long list of clients, including enduring clients
like Liberty Bank, Total Community Action,
The City of New Orleans, Entergy, New Orleans Public Schools, and New Orleans East
Hospital.
In the 1990s and early 2000s, while managing the day-to-day operations of Bright Moments, Bill hosted Sunday Journal radio show
every Sunday from 7 to 9 a.m. on WYLD FM
Radio. He simultaneously hosted a weekly TV
show on the Cox Cable Access Channel
called The Liberty Network—sponsored by
Libelty Bank. Both shows featured news analysis, feature interviews and hard hitting, honest dialogue between the host and the viewing
and listening audience.
One of the City’s leading political strategists,
he managed successful campaigns for Public
School and City millage elections, as well as
numerous political candidates such as Dorothy
Mae Taylor, the first Black woman legislator in
Louisiana, United States Senator—Mary Landrieu, Mayors Ray Nagin, Mitch Landrieu, and
the first female African American Mayor of
New Orleans, LaToya Cantrell, to name a few.
Since Katrina, local, state, and national organizations alike have sought his expertise,
knowledge, and ability to reach into the community. Bright Moments has been instrumental
in ensuring citizen participation in the rebuilding of New Orleans Public Schools, site preparation for new hospitals, creating a Master
Plan for Land Use and a new Comprehensive
Zoning Ordinance, as well as numerous redevelopment efforts.
In 2007, Rouselle was honored with the
local advertising industry’s highest honor, the
Silver Medal, presented by the New Orleans
Ad Club, and in 2021, Rouselle received the

RECOGNIZING THE 50TH ANNIVERSARY
OF
THE
HUNGARIAN
HUMAN RIGHTS FOUNDATION

HON. ANDY HARRIS
OF MARYLAND

IN THE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES

Monday, November 9, 2026
Mr. HARRIS of Maryland. Mr. Speaker, I
rise today to recognize the 50th anniversary of
the Hungarian Human Rights Foundation.
For five decades, the Hungarian Human
Rights Foundation has demonstrated what can
be accomplished when people are willing to
stand up for human dignity, defend fundamental rights, and make sure that the voices
of minority communities are heard.
What began as a small group of dedicated
advocates grew into an organization with a
lasting presence in Washington and an international reputation for documenting human
rights abuses and bringing them to the attention of policymakers. Over the years, the
Foundation has testified before Congress,
worked with American policymakers, and
helped ensure that the rights of Hungarian
communities in Romania, Slovakia, Serbia,
Ukraine, and elsewhere remained part of the
international conversation. Its work was particularly important during the Cold War, when
reliable information about the treatment of
Hungarian minorities behind the Iron Curtain
was often difficult to obtain.
That history is a reminder that defending
human rights is not something that can be
taken for granted. It requires people willing to
speak up, even when doing so is dangerous.
As we celebrate 50 years of the Hungarian
Human Rights Foundation, we should recognize the generations of leaders, volunteers,
and advocates who built this organization and
carried its mission forward. And we should
look toward the next 50 years with the same
determination.
Congratulations to the Hungarian Human
Rights Foundation on this remarkable milestone. I thank them for their service to the
Hungarian people, to the Hungarian-American
community, and to the cause of human rights.
As a proud Hungarian-American, I am honored to join in celebrating the 50th anniversary
of the Hungarian Human Rights Foundation.
Congratulations.

under former Sheriff Louis Hyde and retired as

at the original Parish Prison Facility, he led the

Mr. GARAMENDI. Mr. Speaker, I rise today
to celebrate the 65th anniversary of the Peace
Corps and its enduring commitment to putting
service to work for communities around the
world.
On March 1, 1961, President John F. Kennedy issued his historic call to service and established the Peace Corps, launching a new
era of American volunteerism abroad. Over
the past 65 years, nearly 250,000 Americans
have served as Peace Corps volunteers in
144 countries, fostering people-to-people diplomacy in areas such as education, health,
agriculture, environment, youth in development, and community economic development.
My wife, Patti, and I heard the call of President Kennedy and decided to begin our marriage serving together as Peace Corps volunteers in Ethiopia. Both Patti and I credit our
careers in public service to the hard work and
rewarding service we experienced all those
years ago in Ethiopia.
Today, the Peace Corps continues to exemplify its slogan, ‘‘the toughest job you’ll ever
love,’’ building sustainable partnerships and
strengthening communities around the world.
It has enhanced global perceptions of the
United States by demonstrating American values through service, humility, cultural exchange, and partnership rather than through
political or military means.
Service in the Peace Corps has inspired
generations of Americans to pursue careers in
public service, education, economic development, diplomacy, and health, creating a lasting
pipeline of globally minded civic leaders.
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to celebrate this
momentous 65th anniversary of the Peace
Corps. I rise to honor the more than 250,000
individuals who have served as Peace Corps
volunteers for their dedication to peace, friendship, and community-driven development. I
commend the Peace Corps’ enduring mission
to put purpose, passion, and skills to work for
America and the world.

IN THE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES

Monday, November 9, 2026
Mr. RESCHENTHALER. Mr. Speaker, I rise
to celebrate the retirement of Captain Phillip
A. Chockley from the United States Navy after
23 years of honorable service.
A native of Shelbyville, Tennessee, Captain
Chockley earned a Bachelor of Arts in Philosophy and Political Science from the University
of Tennessee at Martin, a Juris Doctor from
the University of Tennessee, and a Master of
Laws in International and National Security
Law from Columbia University. He received
his commission in October 2002 through the
Student Program. After being admitted to
practice law in Tennessee in 2003, Captain
Chockley attended Officer Indoctrination and
Naval Justice School before beginning his career as a Navy judge advocate.
Captain Chockley’s first duty station was the
Trial Service Office East in Norfolk, VA, where
he served as a command services attorney
and trial counsel. Next, he served as the Deputy Director of Command Services, Assistant
Staff Judge Advocate for Command, Navy Region Europe, and lastly Senior Trial Counsel in
the Regional Legal Service office of Europe
and Southwest Asia, located in Naples, Italy.
In 2009, Captain Chockley deployed to
Baghdad, Iraq, in support of Operation Iraqi
Freedom. There, he served as the Officer in
Charge of the Central Criminal Court of Iraq
Liaison Office. After returning from Iraq, he assumed duty as Flag Secretary to the Deputy
Judge Advocate General of the Navy. Captain
Chockley next served as Deputy Fleet Judge
Advocate at U.S. Third Fleet, providing operational and administrative legal support to the
Commander on a variety of issues facing the
fleet. After concluding his tour at Third Fleet,
Captain Chockley transferred to Norfolk, Virginia, where he served as Staff Judge Advocate to the Eisenhower Carrier Strike Group,
deploying to the Fifth and Sixth Fleet areas of
operations in support of Operation Inherent
Resolve. From Norfolk, Captain Chockley and
his family returned to Europe, where he
served as an Assistant Legal Counsel and
eventually Chief of Operational Law at U.S.
Africa Command in Stuttgart, Germany.

Mr. CARTER of Louisiana. Mr. Speaker, I
rise today to honor Margaret Orr, a New Orleans native and icon, and chief meteorologist,
as she is set to retire after 45 years on the air.
Margaret joined WDSU News in 1979 as a
general assignment reporter. She became cohost of the ‘‘Breakfast Edition’’ with reporter
Bill Stanley, and later co-host of the ‘‘World’s
Fair Show’’ with Alec Gifford. For more than
20 years, Margaret has co-hosted the Children’s Hospital Telethon with Norman Robinson helping to raise millions of dollars for Children’s Hospital.
Margaret grew up in New Orleans where
she graduated from Louise S. McGehee High
School, and Louisiana State University in
Baton Rouge.
In 1965, when Hurricane Betsy blew the
roof off her childhood home, she was mesmerized by her view of the sky when the eye of
the hurricane passed overhead. That kicked

VerDate Sep 11 2014

08:40 Nov 10, 2026

Jkt 079060

off a lifelong obsession with weather events—
and solidified a remarkable ability to always
look for the positive in virtually any scenario.
As her fascination with weather grew, she
completed the Mississippi State Broadcast
Meteorology program with flying colors. Officially bitten by the news bug, she graduated in
1975 and moved up to Charleston, South
Carolina and got a job working at a TV station
as a receptionist. In the evenings, she tagged
along with the news crew and learned how to
use equipment so she could film segments.
Eventually, a position opened, and she worked
there for a few years before relocating to
Baton Rouge, and then eventually getting a
call from WDSU in New Orleans.
In 2009, she began forecasting weather for
the 5, 6 and 10 p.m. news after many years
on the morning news. Margaret Orr is a meteorologist who gained prominence for her work
at WDSU–TV, an NBC affiliate in New Orleans, Louisiana. She has been with the station
for several years, providing weather forecasts
and coverage of significant weather events, including hurricanes. Orr is known for her expertise and dedication to keeping viewers informed and safe during severe weather situations in the Gulf Coast region.
Over the years, she would become a trusted
source of news and weather, helping guide
the city through some of its toughest times, including Hurricane Katrina. While most of the
station evacuated, a small skeleton crew,
which included reporters Roop Raj, Dan
Thomas, Helena Moreno and Orr, remained
behind. As conditions worsened, they were
forced to leave the TV set and seek shelter at
the Hilton New Orleans Riverside Hotel. Orr,
meanwhile, was desperate for the storm to
blow over so she could get outside and start
relaying what she saw to her viewers.
Through her conversational, enthusiastic reporting style, she’s become a larger-than-life
local celebrity—characterized by her signature
red hair and blazers as bright as her fun-loving personality.
Whether it was as a weather forecaster, a
colleague or a friend, Orr has consistently
been there for her community with genuine
care. It has not been uncommon for Orr to become emotional, wearing her heart on her
sleeve, as she urges viewers to heed her
warnings. Margaret is a member of both the
American Meteorology Society and the National Weather Association. She has Seals of
Approval from both. Margaret has also won
first-place awards from the Associated Press
and the New Orleans Press Club for breaking
weather.
When Margaret is not at work, she is likely
tweeting about the weather, something she
plans to continue after retirement. You can follow her on Twitter by following @margaretorr.
She tweets the latest forecast and during severe weather, she gives the latest warnings to
keep you safe.
Margaret is married with three children and
a dog named Bleu. Bleu is royalty—he was
King of Barkus. Margaret likes to garden,
paint, read, swim and bike.
On this day I wish her many happy days
during her retirement. A special salute as she
sends happiness outside of the newsroom.

Mr. CARTER of Louisiana. Mr. Speaker, I
rise today to honor The Honorable Ethel S.
Julien as we celebrate her thirty-year tenure
on the bench. Judge Julien is dear to the citizens of New Orleans and Louisiana’s 2nd
Congressional District.
Judge Julien was born to Mrs. Lucille
Simms and Mr. Alfred Simms. Her mother, an
educator, instilled in Judge Julien and her
brothers. Seymour and Stewart, a profound
reverence for God and an insatiable thirst for
knowledge. She pursued her education at
Valena C. Jones Elementary School, Blessed
Sacrament School, and Xavier Prep High
School, ultimately graduating from Southern
University Law Center. Through divine providence and unwavering dedication, she
achieved the distinction of being the first of
her class to graduate magna cum laude.
Throughout her illustrious legal career, Judge
Julien has been consistently blessed by divine
favor, enabling her to become the longestserving African American judge on the Civil,
District Court.
Judge Julien first worked as an associate at
Jefferson, Bryan, Gray and Jupiter Attorneys
and Counselors at Law from 1983 to 1988.
She then founded the law firm at Julien and
Julien in 1989, alongside her late husband,
Henry Julien, Esq., where she worked as a
partner until her judicial election in 1995. Following her tenure as judge ad hoc in the Orleans Parish Juvenile Court and judge pro tempore in Civil District Court. Division ‘‘A,’’ Judge
Julien was elected in September 1995 as
Judge of the Civil District Court. Division ‘‘N,’’
where she has held office continuously since.
In 2000, the Louisiana Supreme Court appointed her ad hoc to the First Circuit Court of

PO 00000

Frm 00009

Fmt 0626

Sfmt 9920

Appeal to assist in mitigating the court’s docket.
Judge Julien’s tenure on the bench was
both gratifying and arduous. In August 2005,
while serving as Chief Judge of the Civil District Court, Judge Julien assumed the unprecedented responsibility of guiding the court
through the aftermath of Hurricane Katrina.
Despite personal property damage to her residence, she collaborated with displaced judges,
court personnel, and the clerk of court to reopen
court
operations
in
Gonzales,
Donaldsonville, and subsequently St. Tammany Parish. These endeavors afforded litigants the opportunity to have their cases adjudicated while the court was temporarily relocated. Accommodations were secured, and
expedited process was implemented to expedite Katrina-related cases, an achievement
made feasible solely through the collective efforts of the court. Notably, this court became
the inaugural regional entity to reopen and reestablish jury trials. Witnessing prospective jurors lined up, eagerly anticipating a return to
normalcy, was particularly poignant.
Judge Julien has consistently demonstrated
a commitment to community service. She
spearheaded the establishment of scholarship
programs at Austerlitz Street Baptist Church,
the First District Missionary Baptist Association, and the Cornerstone Missionary Baptist
General Association, thereby providing scholarships and book stipends to foster academic
excellence and support students. Furthermore,
she serves as a founding member and president of INSPIRE, RR, an organization dedicated to encouraging students to embark on
their literary journeys through positive reinforcement and rewards.
Judge Julien serves on the Board of the
New Orleans Mission and has held the position of President of the A.P. Tureaud Inn of
Court. She is also a member of numerous attorney and judicial associations. Her tenure on
the bench has been a fulfilling experience, and
she has been unanimously elected for six consecutive terms. Judge Julien envisions that
this continued trust reflects her dedication to
administering justice impartially and equitably.
She acknowledges the confidence bestowed
upon her by the bench, the legal community,
and the citizens of New Orleans. She expresses profound gratitude that both attorneys
and voters have recognized her commitment
to this esteemed role, an honor that she holds
with utmost reverence.
On this day, we celebrate the outstanding
life of service of Judge Ethel Simms Julien.

HONORING THE VETERANS OF
PUERTO RICO

HON. PABLO JOSÉ HERNÁNDEZ
OF PUERTO RICO

IN THE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES

Monday, November 9, 2026
Mr. HERNÁNDEZ. Mr. Speaker, I rise today
to recognize and honor the veterans of Puerto
Rico, whose courage, sacrifice, and devotion
to duty have strengthened the United States of
America for well over a century. Puerto Ricans
have served in the United States Armed
Forces since 1899, when Congress authorized
the creation of the Porto Rico Battalion of Volunteer Infantry, just months after the island
became part of the United States. That unit

E:\CR\FM\A09NO8.032

E09NOPT1

E1174

CONGRESSIONAL RECORD — Extensions of Remarks

grew into the Porto Rico Regiment of Infantry
and, in 1920, was redesignated as the 65th Infantry Regiment. When the Jones Act granted
United States citizenship to the people of
Puerto Rico in 1917, thousands of our young
men answered the call of duty, stepping forward without hesitation to serve in World War
I.
Across every generation since then, the
sons and daughters of Puerto Rico have stood
shoulder to shoulder with their fellow Americans in defense of freedom. They served with
distinction in World War II, the Korean War,
the Vietnam War, the Persian Gulf War, and
the conflicts in Iraq and Afghanistan, as well
as in peacekeeping and humanitarian missions around the world. Among the most celebrated are the members of the 65th Infantry
Regiment, the Borinqueneers, whose bravery
in Korea earned them the Congressional Gold
Medal in 2014. Puerto Rican service members
have received the Medal of Honor and countless other decorations for valor, and Puerto
Rican women have served with honor in every
branch of our Armed Forces.
Their contributions did not end when they
took off the uniform. When they came home,
they became teachers, doctors, public servants, business owners, and community leaders, bringing the discipline, leadership, and
sense of duty they learned in service to every
community on the island. They have raised
families, mentored our young people, and
been among the first to help their neighbors
recover and rebuild after hurricanes and earthquakes. Like so many Puerto Ricans, I grew
up hearing their stories, told with quiet pride
by fathers, grandparents, and uncles who had
worn the uniform. Those stories taught us
what it means to serve something greater than
ourselves.
For more than 125 years, Puerto Rico’s veterans have demonstrated extraordinary patriotism and selflessness. Their sacrifices have
helped secure the liberties that Puerto Ricans
and all Americans enjoy, and their legacy remains a source of pride for the people of
Puerto Rico and for the entire country. As we
approach Veterans Day, we have a solemn responsibility not only to thank them, but to ensure they receive the care, benefits, and recognition they have earned.
Mr. Speaker, I ask my colleagues to join me
in recognizing the veterans of Puerto Rico and
in expressing our deepest gratitude for their
courage, their sacrifice, and their enduring

HON. TROY A. CARTER

IN THE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES

Mr. CARTER of Louisiana. Mr. Speaker, I
rise today to celebrate three decades of faithful, phenomenal leadership from an outstanding New Orleans Minister, Pastor Reginald Nicholas, Sr. Pastor Reginald Nicholas,
Sr. is the 12th Presiding Pastor of the Olive
Branch Baptist Church and was born on April
12, 1968, to the late Arthur Matthews and
Irma Nicholas. Pastor Nicholas was reared by
his grandparents, Herbert and Francis Wallace. He accepted Christ on April 12, 1968,
and was baptized at St. Paul Missionary Baptist Church by his late great uncle, Pastor
Haywood Custer.
In 1980, he became a proud member of
New Jerusalem Baptist Church under the
leadership of Pastor Emeritus George Davis
Sr. While at New Jerusalem, Pastor Nicholas
served under the leadership of Pastor George
Davis Sr. It was there he grew in the grace of
God while serving as Director of Brotherhood
and Foreign Mission; Co-Chairman of the
Deacon Board; Sunday School and Bible
Study Teacher. In August 1986, he was called
to the Ministry. On October 12, 1986, Pastor
Nicholas preached his first sermon, ‘‘Never
Look Down on a Man, unless you are Picking
Him Up’’. He was ordained on July 30, 1988.
Pastor Nicholas received a Bachelor of Theology, Master of Biblical Studies, Graduate
Specialist, and Doctor of Theology from Christian Bible College of Louisiana.
On Thursday, June 30, 1994, he was selected to Pastor Olive Branch Baptist and installed on July 15, 1994, by the Westside Missionary Baptist Association. Pastor Nicholas
serves faithfully and untiringly as a dedicated
Pastor, ministering to all the needs of this congregation, visiting the sick, attending to widows, and ministering to those in prison.
Pastor Nicholas is a community-oriented
leader. In January 1995, he organized the 1st
Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. March in Algiers, inviting two of Dr. King’s nephews, Derrick and
Vernon C. King.
In 2000, Pastor Reginald Nicholas, Sr., the
late Pastors Arthur Wardsworth, and Randy
Stevenson organized WSN Ministries, Inc., a
family ministry designed to help strengthen
families and teach them to deal with different
issues biblically.

CELEBRATING THE ACCOMPLISHMENTS OF BRYAN CHRISTOPHER
‘‘BIRDMAN’’ WILLIAMS

HON. TROY A. CARTER
OF LOUISIANA

IN THE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES

Monday, November 9, 2026
Mr. CARTER of Louisiana. Mr. Speaker,
today, I rise to highlight the achievements of
a Louisiana Great, Mr. Bryan Christopher Williams, best known as ‘‘Birdman’’ or ‘‘Baby.’’ I
am truly honored by his contributions to
Bounce Music. He has made a lasting impact
on the music industry, as co-founder of Cash
Money Records, a record executive, and artist,
along with his brother Ronald ‘‘Slim’’ Williams.
Born February 15, 1969, in my hometown of
New Orleans, Louisiana to Johnnie Williams
and Gladys Brooks, Williams did not sign the
birth certificate, which led to Bryan initially taking his mother’s surname. For nearly a month
after his birth, he did not have a first name
and was referred to as ‘‘Baby,’’ a nickname he
has retained to this day. As a child, Bryan and
his family lived atop a bar owned by his family. His mother was tragically murdered when
he was two years old, and following her death,
Bryan and his siblings were sent to live with
a relative in Prince George, British Columbia,
Canada. After spending two years in the foster
care system, his father was granted legal custody of his children in the mid-1970s. Shortly
thereafter, Bryan’s surname was changed to
Williams. He, along with his siblings, lived in
the Magnolia Projects in Central City in the
3rd Ward of Uptown New Orleans. His father,
Johnnie Williams, passed away in 1996.
In the late 1980s, Bounce Music emerged
on the scene. Bounce Music, like many other
genres, is derived from hip-hop. This sound,
like non-other, captivated club goers throughout New Orleans. In 1992, Baby and Slim

E:\CR\FM\A09NO8.039

E09NOPT1

E1176

CONGRESSIONAL RECORD — Extensions of Remarks

formed Cash Money Records, and signed their
first artist, a local rapper names ‘‘Kilo G,’’ who
released their label’s first project titled ‘‘The
Sleepwalker.’’ The nightclubs in New Orleans
became a hub for local talent. Baby and Slim
would travel around the city looking for new
talent to join the Cash Money Record Label.
Bryan convinced his friend DJ Mannie Fresh
to serve as the label’s in-house producer.
By the mid-1990s, Cash Money Records
popularity greatly increased as an independent
label in the South. In 1995, 12-year-old
Dwayne Carter was discovered at a local
block party by Cash Money artist Lil Slim.
Shortly after, Dwayne was signed to the label,
making him the youngest artist signed.
Dwayne and 14-year-old rapper Christoper
Dorsey formed the group ‘‘The B.G.’z’’ under
the names Baby D and Lil Doogie. They eventually would rename themselves ‘‘Lil Wayne
and B.G.’’ in 1997. Later that year, Baby and
Slim recruited Turk and Juvenile, along with Lil
Wayne and B.G. to form the Hot Boys. The
Hot Boys elevated Cash Money Records to
new heights and because of their success in
1998, the label signed a $30 million deal with
Universal Records
As their popularity grew, more people realized that the South indeed had something to
say. Baby and Mannie Fresh joined forces in
the studio to form ‘‘Big Tymers.’’ Big Tymers
debuted in 1998 with the album How Ya Luv
That?, I Got That Work, in 2000, and Hood
Rich in 2002. ‘‘Get Your Roll On’’ and ‘‘#1
Stunna’’ are popular songs that appeared on
I Got That Work. I Got That Work was certified
platinum by the Recording Industry Association (RIAA) for selling over 1 million copies in
the United States.
I am happy to celebrate Bryan ‘‘Baby/Birdman’’ Williams for his amazing contributions to
amplifying New Orleans Bounce Music Nationally, extending sincerest wishes that he continues to flourish in his future endeavors both
in Louisiana and abroad.

Committee Meetings
RETIREMENT FAIRNESS FOR CHARITIES
AND EDUCATIONAL INSTITUTIONS ACT
OF 2025
Committee on Rules: Full Committee held a hearing on
H.R. 1013, the ‘‘Retirement Fairness for Charities
and Educational Institutions Act of 2025’’. The
Committee granted, by a record vote of 7–3, a rule
providing for consideration of H.R. 1013, the ‘‘Retirement Fairness for Charities and Educational Institutions Act of 2025’’, under a closed rule. The rule
waives all points of order against consideration of the
bill. The rule provides that the amendment in the
nature of a substitute recommended by the Committee on Financial Services now printed in the bill
shall be considered as adopted and the bill, as
amended, shall be considered as read. The rule
waives all points of order against provisions in the
bill, as amended. The rule provides one hour of general debate equally divided and controlled by the
chair and ranking minority member of the Committee on Financial Services or their respective designees. Finally, the rule provides one motion to recommit. Testimony was heard from Representatives
Davidson and Waters.

Joint Meetings
No joint committee meetings were held.

The Congressional Record (USPS 087–390). The Periodicals postage
is paid at Washington, D.C. The public proceedings of each House
of Congress, as reported by the Official Reporters thereof, are
printed pursuant to directions of the Joint Committee on Printing as authorized by appropriate provisions of Title 44, United
States Code, and published for each day that one or both Houses are in session, excepting very infrequent instances when
two or more unusually small consecutive issues are printed one time. ¶ Public access to the Congressional Record is available online through
the U.S. Government Publishing Office, at www.govinfo.gov, free of charge to the user. The information is updated online each day the
Congressional Record is published. For more information, contact the GPO Customer Contact Center, U.S. Government Publishing Office.
Phone 202–512–1800, or 866–512–1800 (toll-free). E-Mail, contactcenter@gpo.gov. ¶ To place an order for any of these products, visit the U.S.
Government Online Bookstore at: bookstore.gpo.gov. Mail orders to: Superintendent of Documents, P.O. Box 979050, St. Louis, MO
63197–9000, or phone orders to 866–512–1800 (toll-free), 202–512–1800 (D.C. area), or fax to 202–512–2104. Remit check or money order, made
payable to the Superintendent of Documents, or use VISA, MasterCard, Discover, American Express, or GPO Deposit Account. ¶ Following
each session of Congress, the daily Congressional Record is revised, printed, permanently bound and sold by the Superintendent of Documents
in individual parts or by sets. ¶ With the exception of copyrighted articles, there are no restrictions on the republication of material from
the Congressional Record.
